Eliphelet: a Hebrew name, meaning "God has delivered him". He was the son of Eshek of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr 8:39).
And the sons of Ulam were mighty men of valour, archers, and had many sons, and sons' sons, an hundred and fifty.

All these are of the sons of Benjamin. [40] 1. It is noted in the genealogies of all the tribes that there is no reference to any king of Israel after the split from the house of David. Nor did it say anything about the house of Jeroboam, Baasha, Omri and Jehu, because all of these were idolaters. 2. He took care of the descendants of Jonathan son of Saul, perhaps because of his loyalty and faithfulness in his friendship with David. 3. The genealogies ended with Ulam and his sons, whose family became especially famous in the tribe of Benjamin because of the multitude of his sons and his sons' sons, who numbered a hundred and fifty, known as mighty men of valour. The secret of their greatness is not in their authority or social positions or wealth, but in their service to their country, because they were mighty men of valour in battles.
In the midst of dense thorns You present to us beautiful roses!
v It was not possible for the tribes of Israel to imagine the corruption that Benjamin had reached (Judg 19-20).
The sons of Benjamin became the corrupt sons of Belial.
In foulness they abused the Levite's concubine all night long.
In the morning they found her fallen at the door of the house, dead, with her hands upon the threshold.
The Levite divided her body and distributed it among the tribes.
The tribes rushed upon Benjamin, and almost destroyed the whole tribe (Judg 21:3).
v From this tribe arose King Saul, who disobeyed the Lord.
He neglected the ark of the covenant, and in his distress consulted the spirits, not the Lord.
What bitterness came upon all the people of God because of this tribe!
v In the midst of these dangerous thorns God tended beautiful roses, bearing the fragrance of love and holiness.
What a flower God cared for, like Jonathan son of Saul.
He did not care to inherit the throne from his father, since the Lord had chosen David, the man of God, as heir to the throne!
He loved David as his own soul, and gave him his robe and his sword.
He spared no effort to rescue the sweet psalmist of Israel from the hands of Saul his wicked father!
v Many of Saul's relatives, men of valour, for the sake of the Lord left Saul and clung to David.
They preceded many of the tribes in making David king over all Israel.
They became David's men and his guard, because he is a man of God.
v When the tribes ran after Jeroboam, who split the kingdom of Israel,
Benjamin was determined to cling to the kingdom of Judah.
What roses of love, sincerity and faithfulness to God and to His commandments and His dispensations they were.

v Truly Benjamin bears witness on the great Day of the Lord that the Lord planted them as a delightful garden bearing the sweet fragrance of Christ, in the midst of a tribe with its errors and grave sins!
v Teach me not to despise any community because of the corrupt in it.
For in the midst of pitch darkness the light of Your grace shines on many!
In the midst of deep darkness brilliant stars glitter, bearing witness to Your grace.

entries.section: 1. Heads of fathers from the captivity

paragraphs.text: 1 So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel. And Judah was carried away to Babylon for their transgression. 2 Now the first inhabitants that dwelt in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, Levites, and the Nethinims. 3 And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim, and Manasseh; 4 Uthai the son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, the son of Bani, of the children of Pharez the son of Judah. 5 And of the Shilonites; Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons. 6 And of the sons of Zerah; Jeuel, and their brethren, six hundred and ninety. 7 And of the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hasenuah, 8 And Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, and Elah the son of Uzzi, the son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephathiah, the son of Reuel, the son of Ibnijah; 9 And their brethren, according to their generations, nine hundred and fifty and six. All these men were chief of the fathers in the house of their fathers.
So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel.
And Judah was carried away to Babylon for their transgression. [1]

Here he looks back to the genealogies mentioned before, and tells us that they were gathered from the books of the kings of Israel and Judah, not those books included in the Bible, but in the civil records, which are reliable records.
With man's personal responsibility for his works, he must also pray for the sanctification of the community as a whole, so that God's wrath may not come upon all.
All Israel: here Israel together with Judah is meant.
The captivity took place because of the people's fall as a whole into idol worship, despite the Lord's continual warnings to them through the prophets.

Even those of them who had not turned aside to idol worship were exposed to falling into the captivity. Therefore it befits the believer to cry to God in repentance and return to Him, not for himself or his family only, but for the whole community as well. Truly we are not judged for the sins of others, even if they are the closest to us, but in love we must desire, ask for and do whatever we can for the salvation of all.

entries.section: 1. Heads of fathers from the captivity

paragraphs.text: Now the first inhabitants that dwelt in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, Levites, and the Nethinims. [2]
The first inhabitants: most likely meaning those who were first in the return from the captivity, because this chapter resembles the eleventh chapter of Nehemiah.
They are Israel, the priests, etc. That is, the people and the priests, etc.

The Nethinim: a Hebrew name meaning "dedicated". It occurs in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, and it means the Gentiles who were assigned to the service of the Temple, such as the Gibeonites (Josh 9:3, 27), and the Midianite captives (Num 31:2, 47), and those whom David appointed with the princes for the service of the Temple and the service of the Levitical priests (Ezra 8:20), and they were hewers of wood and drawers of water. Although David is the one who established the office of the Nethinim, it is thought that the name attached to them later, and the name occurs only in the days of Nehemiah and Ezra, and once in First Chronicles (1 Chr 9:2). The number of the Nethinim was not sufficient to perform all the services of the Temple, especially in the days of Solomon.

entries.section: 1. Heads of fathers from the captivity

paragraphs.text: And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim, and Manasseh; [3]
The most important of those returning from the captivity were the tribes of Judah and Benjamin (Ezra 1:5).

Jerusalem: it was not a part of the Promised Land in the time of Joshua son of Nun, and it was not distributed among the tribes, but remained in the possession of the Canaanites and particularly the Jebusites, and was called "Jebus". It was a fortified city, difficult to storm. David's forces were able to storm it in 992 BC, and David made it the capital of the kingdom (2 Sam 5:6-7). For this reason we find that the city of Jerusalem, unlike the rest of the cities, was inhabited by Israelites from many tribes [3].

Since the ark of the covenant was carried to it after it became the capital, Jerusalem became a religious center, and after the building of the Temple in the days of Solomon it became a dwelling for many priests and Levites and other liturgical servants [10-12].
By the sons of Benjamin and the sons of Ephraim and Manasseh are meant people from these tribes near Jerusalem in the north, who worshipped the Lord and united with Judah (2 Chr 30:10, 18).

entries.section: 1. Heads of fathers from the captivity

paragraphs.text: Uthai the son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, the son of Bani, of the children of Pharez the son of Judah. [4]

Uthai (Utai): a Hebrew name, meaning "Jehovah surpassed". It is the name of a son of Ammihud, of the sons of Pharez son of Judah. He was one of those who returned to Jerusalem after the captivity (1 Chr 9:4).

Ammihud: a Hebrew name, meaning "my uncle is majestic". He was the son of Omri, one of the descendants of Pharez, of the sons of Judah; his son Uthai returned to Jerusalem after the captivity (1 Chr 9:4).
Omri: a Hebrew name, perhaps meaning "prosperous". He was the son of Imri son of Pharez, of the sons of Judah (1 Chr 9:4).
Imri: a Hebrew name, an abbreviation of Amariah. It is the name of a son of Bani of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 9:4).
Bani: a Hebrew name, meaning "builder". Perhaps it is an abbreviation of "Benaiah", and he was of the tribe of Judah.
Pharez: a Hebrew name, meaning "breach".

entries.section: 1. Heads of fathers from the captivity

paragraphs.text: And of the Shilonites; Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons. [5]
Asaiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "Jehovah has made". He was the firstborn of the Shilonite (1 Chr 9:5), and he was of the sons of Judah, and was living at the return from the captivity.
The Shilonites: the inhabitants of Shiloh. And of a family in Judah that dwelt in Jerusalem after the captivity (1 Chr 9:5).

entries.section: 1. Heads of fathers from the captivity

paragraphs.text: And of the sons of Zerah; Jeuel, and their brethren, six hundred and ninety. [6]

Jeuel: a Hebrew name, meaning "he heals, he keeps". More than one person bears this name, among them: 1. The father of Gibeon, a Benjamite among the forefathers of Saul (1 Chr 9:35). 2. A man of the descendants of Judah (1 Chr 9:6).

entries.section: 1. Heads of fathers from the captivity

paragraphs.text: And of the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hasenuah [7]
Sallu: a Hebrew name, meaning "faithful forthwith, or consecrated". He was a man of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr 9:7).

Meshullam: a Hebrew name, meaning "one who has received his recompense". More than one person bears this name, among them: 1. Persons of the sons of Benjamin: Meshullam son of Hodaviah [7]; and Meshullam son of Shephathiah [8]. 2. One of the priests: Meshullam son of Zadok (1 Chr 9:11). 3. A priest of the family of Immer: Meshullam son of Meshillemith son of Immer (1 Chr 9:12).
Hodaviah: a Hebrew name, meaning "glory to Jehovah". He was the son of Hasenuah, of the sons of Benjamin (1 Chr 9:7).
Hasenuah: a Hebrew name, meaning "the hated". He was a man of Benjamin, the son of Hodaviah (1 Chr 9:7).

entries.section: 1. Heads of fathers from the captivity

paragraphs.text: And Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, and Elah the son of Uzzi, the son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephathiah, the son of Reuel, the son of Ibnijah; [8]
Ibneiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "Jehovah builds". The son of Jeroham and the father of Reuel, of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr 9:8), and perhaps they are two persons.
Elah: a Hebrew name, meaning oak tree. He is the name of a son of Uzzi of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr 9:8).
Michri: a Hebrew name, perhaps meaning "price". He was a Benjamite, the grandfather of Elah (1 Chr 9:8).
Shephathiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "Jehovah has given judgment". He was a Benjamite who dwelt in Jerusalem after the captivity (1 Chr 9:8).
Reuel: a Hebrew name, meaning "friend of God". He was a Benjamite chief (1 Chr 9:8).

entries.section: 1. Heads of fathers from the captivity

paragraphs.text: And their brethren, according to their generations, nine hundred and fifty and six.
All these men were chief of the fathers in the house of their fathers. [9]

Perhaps the names mentioned here are of those who returned to Jerusalem and were occupied with the worship of God with burning zeal. The Temple had not yet been rebuilt, yet this did not lead them to neglect the worship of God.

10 And of the priests; Jedaiah, and Jehoiarib, and Jachin, 11 And Azariah the son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, the ruler of the house of God; 12 And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer; 13 And their brethren, heads of the house of their fathers, a thousand and seven hundred and threescore; very able men for the work of the service of the house of God.
And of the priests; Jedaiah, and Jehoiarib, and Jachin [10]
Jedaiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "Jehovah knows".

Jehoiarib: a Hebrew name, meaning "Jehovah contends, strives". He was of the descendants of Aaron, whose course was made the first of the courses of the priests in the days of David. His family dwelt in Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:10).
Jachin: a Hebrew name, meaning "he establishes". He was the head of the twenty-first course of the courses of the priests in Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:10).
And Azariah the son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, the ruler of the house of God; [11]
Azariah: a Hebrew name, meaning "whom Jehovah has helped". He was the son of Hilkiah, and the father of Seraiah, and he was a great priest (1 Chr 9:11).

What occupies the heart of God is a person's faithfulness, not the kind of service or his position or his rank. Azariah received special attention although his role or work was to oversee the cleanliness of the Temple.

The Bible took care to mention his name in the genealogies as it took care to mention the names of the priests and Levites who carried out the works of teaching and praise and some positions of leadership which have an honoured appearance before people. God's esteem of man is not in his role in work or his position in society, but in the purity of his heart, his cleanness, his sincerity and faithfulness. Therefore the Lord's praise of those on the right hand on the great Day of the Lord: "You have been faithful over a few things, I will make you ruler over many things: enter into the joy of your lord" (Mt 25:21).
Hilkiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "Jehovah is my portion, my share".
Zadok: a Hebrew name, meaning "just or righteous". He was a priest of the line of the high priests, the father of Shallum and the son of the second Ahitub, of the second Meraioth (1 Chr 9:11).
Meraioth: "rebellion". He is the name of a priest, and he is the son of Ahitub (1 Chr 9:11).
Ahitub: a Hebrew name, meaning "brother of goodness".
And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer [12]
Adaiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "from the adornment of Jehovah". He was the son of Jeroham son of Malchijah, one of the priests (1 Chr 9:12).

Jeroham: a Hebrew name, meaning "he whom God has mercy upon or whom He pleases". He was a Benjamite, the father of Ibneiah, who was dwelling in Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:8). A priest of the house of Malchijah (1 Chr 9:10, 12).
Pashur: perhaps an Egyptian name meaning "portion of the god Horus". The founder of one of the families of the priests, some of whose members returned from the Babylonian captivity (1 Chr 9:12).
Malchijah: a Hebrew name, meaning "Jehovah is king".
Maasiai: a Hebrew name, meaning "work of Jehovah". He was a priest (1 Chr 9:12).
Adiel: a Hebrew name, meaning "adornment to God". He was the son of Jahzerah, the father of Maasiai, one of the heads of the priestly families (1 Chr 9:12).
Jahzerah: a Hebrew name, meaning "cautious".
Meshillemith: a Hebrew name, meaning "punishment". He was a priest of the line of Immer (1 Chr 9:12).

Immer: a Hebrew word meaning "sheep". The name of a priest in the age of David appears, and the sixteenth course of the priests was of his descendants. Perhaps he was the forefather of the priests mentioned in (1 Chr 9:12).
And their brethren, heads of the house of their fathers, a thousand and seven hundred and threescore; very able men for the work of the service of the house of God. [13]

They were mighty men of valour not in fighting nor in material resources, but in their seriousness in serving the house of the Lord and resisting error. We are accustomed to hear of "mighty men of valour" for entering into battles with enemies to overcome them, but here the heads of their fathers' houses are required to be mighty men of valour for the work of the service of the house of God. As if the house of God were a battlefield, and it befits the servants of God to be mighty men of valour who stand against the devil himself and the powers of darkness.

14 And of the Levites; Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari; 15 And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph; 16 And Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, the son of Elkanah, that dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites.

The Levites practiced praise or singing with exact arrangement and order, as there were 24 courses for this work. Praise was not a job from which the singers made a living, but a worship issuing from hearts consecrated to the Lord and sanctified to Him, whose message is to give an experience of the pledge of the heavenly life. The Levite singers were fathers who offered the people a life of joy and exultation, finding their happiness in the happiness of the people in God, the source of joy.
And of the Levites; Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari. [14]
Shemaiah: it means "Jehovah hears". He is a Levite of the descendants of Burni. He was overseer of the outward business of the house of God in the days of Nehemiah (1 Chr 9:14).
Hasshub: a Hebrew name, perhaps meaning "he who is thought of, or toward whom God's thought turns". A Merarite Levite, the father of Shemaiah (1 Chr 9:14).

Azrikam: a Hebrew name, meaning "my help has risen". More than one person bears this name, among them: 1. The son of Azel, one of the descendants of Jehonathan son of Saul (1 Chr 9:44). 2. The son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari, a Levite (1 Chr 9:14).
Hashabiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "Jehovah has devised or reckoned". Perhaps he was of the descendants of Buni, mentioned as an ancestor of Shemaiah (1 Chr 9:14).
And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph; [15]
Bakbakkar: a Hebrew name, meaning "searcher". He was a Levite man (1 Chr 9:15).
Heresh: a Hebrew name, meaning "dumb, deaf". The head of a Levite clan, attached to the officers of the tabernacle in 445 BC (1 Chr 9:15).
Galal: a Hebrew name, meaning "the Lord has rolled". He was a Levite (1 Chr 9:15). More than one person bears this name, among them: 1. A Levite (1 Chr 9:15). 2. A second Levite (1 Chr 9:16).
Mattaniah: a Hebrew name, meaning "gift of Jehovah". He was a Levite singer of the sons of Asaph (1 Chr 9:15).

Micah: a Hebrew name, meaning "Who is like Jehovah?" More than one person bears this name, among them: 1. The son of Mephibosheth or Meribaal, and grandson of Jonathan (1 Chr 9:40-41). 2. A Levite, son of Zichri or Zabdi son of Asaph (1 Chr 9:15).
Zichri: a Hebrew name, meaning "remembered". He was a Levite (1 Chr 9:15).

Asaph: a Hebrew name, meaning "brother of Manah" or "gift". He was one of the Levites, gatekeepers of the Temple, and in his charge was the guarding of the east gate by which the king entered (1 Chr 9:15, 17).
And Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, the son of Elkanah, that dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites. [16]

Most of those returning from the captivity of the priests and Levites dwelt in Jerusalem [34], but some of them were found who dwelt in the villages, perhaps because they did not find a place for themselves in Jerusalem.

Obadiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "festival (servant) of Jehovah". More than one person bears this name, among them: 1. The son of Azel, of the descendants of Jehoshaphat son of Saul (1 Chr 9:44). 2. The son of Shemaiah, of the descendants of Elkanah, who dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites (1 Chr 9:16). 3. A Levite, one of the gatekeepers of the Temple in the days of Nehemiah the governor (Neh 11:17; 12:25). Perhaps he was the same Obadiah son of Shemaiah (1 Chr 9:16).

Jeduthun: a Hebrew name, meaning "praising, one who praises". He was a Levite, and one of the three great singers or musicians whom David appointed, and the founder of a musical family for worship in the Temple. Jeduthun's course was in the Temple after its completion, and also after the captivity (1 Chr 9:16).
Berechiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "blessed of God". He was a Levite, the son of Asa (1 Chr 9:16).

Asa: a Hebrew name, meaning "the healer", that is, "the physician". Perhaps the name is an abbreviation of "Jehovah healed", that is, "the Lord healed and cured". It is the name of a Levite, the son of Elkanah, who dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites after the return from the Babylonian captivity (1 Chr 9:16).
Elkanah: a Hebrew name, meaning "God has created or acquired". He was a Levite who dwelt in one of the villages of the Netophathites (1 Chr 9:16).

The Netophathites, Netophah: a Hebrew name meaning "munaffit". It is a town in Judah near Bethlehem (1 Chr 2:54; Neh 7:26), and after the end of the captivity fifty-six of its inhabitants returned to it. At the beginning it was not of the portion of the Levites, but some of them dwelt in it after the captivity, as some singers dwelt in it (1 Chr 9:16).
And perhaps it was at Khirbet Bedd Falouh near Ain Netuf, to the south of Bethlehem by five generations.

17 And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief; 18 Who hitherto waited in the king's gate eastward: they were porters in the companies of the children of Levi. 19 And Shallum the son of Kore, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah, and his brethren, of the house of his father, the Korahites, were over the work of the service, keepers of the gates of the tabernacle: and their fathers, being over the host of the LORD, were keepers of the entry. 20 And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the ruler over them in time past, and the LORD was with him. 21 And Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was porter of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. 22 All these which were chosen to be porters in the gates were two hundred and twelve. These were reckoned by their genealogy in their villages, whom David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office. 23 So they and their children had the oversight of the gates of the house of the LORD, namely, the house of the tabernacle, to keep guard. 24 In four quarters were the porters, toward the east, west, north, and south. 25 And their brethren, which were in their villages, were to come after seven days from time to time with them. 26 For these Levites, the four chief porters, were in their set office, and were over the chambers and treasuries of the house of God. 27 And they lodged round about the house of God, because the charge was upon them, and the opening thereof every morning pertained to them.

The gatekeepers hold the place of precedence among the officials of worship [17-26]. Their offices go back to the time of the wilderness [19-21], and they continued their work in the days of Samuel and David in the tabernacle [23]. Their faithfulness is praised [22], and they are all of the line of Korah[2].
And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief; [17]

Ahiman: a Hebrew name, meaning "brother of Manah or gift". He was one of the Levites, gatekeepers of the Temple, and in his charge was the guarding of the east gate by which the king entered (1 Chr 9:17).
Who hitherto waited in the king's gate eastward:
they were porters in the companies of the children of Levi. [18]

The keepers of the gates: they used to guard the four entrances of the Temple, and open the gates every morning for those entering for worship, and close them in the evening. They also carried out the daily works of preparing the Temple continually, such as cleaning and preparing the offerings for the sacrifices. They were also responsible that nothing unclean should enter the Temple, and they prevented those entering from behaving in a way not befitting the sanctity of the Temple. They also directed those entering the Temple to the required places. And they were entrusted with the storehouses of the Temple.
It befits all who work in the house of the Lord, whether in devotional, administrative or cleaning work, to be marked by sincerity and faithfulness.
And Shallum the son of Kore, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah, and his brethren, of the house of his father,
the Korahites, were over the work of the service, keepers of the gates of the tabernacle: and their fathers, being over the host of the LORD, were keepers of the entry. [19]
The office of the gatekeepers and others in the service of the house of the Lord was inherited by the sons from the fathers. The beginning of this organization was in the reign of King David.
Kore: a Hebrew name, meaning "partridge". The name of a Korahite, the father of Shallum and Meshelemiah (1 Chr 9:19).
Ebiasaph: a Hebrew name, meaning "my father has gathered or increased".
Korah: a Hebrew name, meaning "terror". The descendants of Korah lived and became famous in the service of the Temple (1 Chr 9:19).
The Korahites: the descendants of Korah son of Izhar son of Kohath son of Levi, and among them were gatekeepers (1 Chr 9:31).
And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the ruler over them in time past, and the LORD was with him. [20]
Phinehas: an Egyptian name meaning "the Nubian". He was the chief over the keepers of the gates of the tabernacle, he is Phinehas son of Eleazar, whose weapon was "the Lord is with him" [20].
He is most likely different from Phinehas the high priest, the son of Eleazar, who was zealous for the sanctity of the Temple (Num 25:7).
Eleazar: a Hebrew name meaning "God has helped".
And Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was porter of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. [21]
Meshelemiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "whom Jehovah rewards". He was the father of a gatekeeper of the tabernacle of meeting in the days of David (1 Chr 9:21).
All these which were chosen to be porters in the gates were two hundred and twelve. These were reckoned by their genealogy in their villages.
Whom David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office. [22]
No one was permitted to be counted among the keepers of the Temple unless he was registered in the genealogical records proving that he was of the descendants of Abraham.
Although Samuel the prophet died before David was installed as king, it is clear that he took part in arranging the worship, though this is not mentioned in another place.
So they and their children had the oversight of the gates of the house of the LORD, namely, the house of the tabernacle, to keep guard. [23]

The priests and Levites devoted much time and effort to worship, with care for many of the instruments of the service. And their families did many works so that worship might be practiced "decently and in order" (1 Cor 14:40). All worked so that the people, when they came to worship, would feel that they were meeting the King of kings in preparation worthy of Him.
In four quarters were the porters, toward the east, west, north, and south. [24]

Many of the Levites worked as gatekeepers, keeping guard [23] at the gates and entrances. King David longed to stand with them, saying: "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness" (Ps 84:10).
And their brethren, which were in their villages, were to come after seven days from time to time with them. [25]

The gatekeepers used to relieve one another on the Sabbath, so one group went and another group took its place. They lived in their villages until the time of their turn of service came, and then they came to Jerusalem.
For these Levites, the four chief porters, were in their set office, and were over the chambers and treasuries of the house of God. [26]
And they lodged round about the house of God, because the charge was upon them, and the opening thereof every morning pertained to them. [27]

28 And certain of them had the charge of the ministering vessels, that they should bring them in and out by tale. 29 Some of them also were appointed to oversee the vessels, and all the instruments of the sanctuary, and the fine flour, and the wine, and the frankincense, and the spices. 30 And some of the sons of the priests made the ointment of the spices. 31 And Mattithiah, one of the Levites, who was the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, had the set office over the things that were made in the pans. 32 And other of their brethren, of the sons of the Kohathites, were over the shewbread, to prepare it every sabbath.
And certain of them had the charge of the ministering vessels, that they should bring them in and out by tale. [28]
They brought in the vessels by count, because they were very precious (Ezra 8:24-34).
Some of them also were appointed to oversee the vessels, and all the instruments of the sanctuary, and the fine flour, and the wine, and the frankincense, and the spices. [29]
And some of the sons of the priests made the ointment of the spices. [30]
And Mattithiah, one of the Levites, who was the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, had the set office over the things that were made in the pans. [31]
Mattithiah: a Hebrew name, meaning "gift of Jehovah". It is the name of a Korahite Levite, appointed over the work of the cooked things (1 Chr 9:31).

Shallum: a Hebrew name, meaning "recompense". The chief of the gatekeepers of the sanctuaries (1 Chr 9:17-18). He was the son of Kore. He and his family worked in guarding the sanctuaries (1 Chr 9:19).

One of the members of the family of the high priests who were of Zadok, and a predecessor of Ezra. He lived before the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. He is the one called "Meshullam" in (1 Chr 9:11).
And other of their brethren, of the sons of the Kohathites, were over the shewbread, to prepare it every sabbath. [32]
They used to remove the old bread on the Sabbath day, and put the new (Lev 24:8).

33 And these are the singers, chief of the fathers of the Levites, who remaining in the chambers were free: for they were employed in that work day and night. 34 These chief fathers of the Levites were chief throughout their generations; these dwelt at Jerusalem.
And these are the singers, chief of the fathers of the Levites, who remaining in the chambers were free: for they were employed in that work day and night. [33]
They were exempt from other work, or from tribute, or military service.

There was a company or several courses for praising God, not for a few minutes or hours in the day, but praising God by day and night. These were great leaders, heads of the families of the Levites. The service of praise is not a secondary service, but an essential work, which raises the people as well as the leaders to the heavenly angelic service. Therefore it befits that it be practiced not as a kind of amusement or entertainment, but as a living encounter with God whom the heavenly orders praise.
These chief fathers of the Levites
were chief throughout their generations;
these dwelt at Jerusalem. [34]
The singers were fully devoted to the work day and night, dwelling in Jerusalem. So praise was a perpetual work, to give a joyful heavenly atmosphere.

35 And in Gibeon dwelt the father of Gibeon, Jehiel, whose wife's name was Maachah: 36 And his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, and Kish, and Baal, and Ner, and Nadab, 37 And Gedor, and Ahio, and Zechariah, and Mikloth. 38 And Mikloth begat Shimeam. And they also dwelt over against their brethren in Jerusalem, with their brethren. 39 And Ner begat Kish; and Kish begat Saul; and Saul begat Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Esh-baal. 40 And the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal: and Merib-baal begat Micah. 41 And the sons of Micah were, Pithon, and Melech, and Tahrea, and Ahaz. 42 And Ahaz begat Jarah; and Jarah begat Alemeth, and Azmaveth, and Zimri; and Zimri begat Moza; 43 And Moza begat Binea; and Rephaiah his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son. 44 And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, then Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan: these were the sons of Azel.
And in Gibeon dwelt the father of Gibeon, Jehiel, whose wife's name was Maachah: [35]
We note that what is stated here [35-44] reveals commitment to order and decency in the service of the house of the Lord (1 Cor 14:40).
The writer returned to the genealogies of Saul in order to prepare for the battle of Gilboa [1000 BC] at the beginning of the next chapter. David took the throne through Saul's death in this battle.

Gibeon: a Hebrew name, meaning "hill", the main city of the Hivites of the people of Canaan. And after several centuries, when Saul killed the Gibeonites, justice was exacted from his seven sons, and they were hanged. Gibeon became of the portion of Benjamin. It was also given with its pasture lands to the sons of Aaron. And the ancestors of Saul dwelt there for a time, and they had influence (1 Chr 9:35).
Maachah: a Semitic name, meaning "injustice". She was the wife of Jeuel the father of Gibeon, from whom Saul descended (1 Chr 9:35).
And his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, and Kish, and Baal, and Ner, and Nadab [36]
Abdon: a Hebrew name, meaning "the enslaved". He was a Benjamite, son of Jeuel the Gibeonite (1 Chr 9:36).
Zur: a Semitic name, meaning "rock". He was the son of the founder of Gibeon (1 Chr 9:36).

Baal, the Baal, and its plural Baalim: a Semitic name, meaning "lord or master or husband". He was a Canaanite god, and was the son of the god El and husband of the goddess Baalah or Asherah or Anath or Ashtoreth, and is known as the god Hadad. He was the god of the farms and lord of fertility in the fields and among the animals and cattle.
Ner: a Hebrew name, meaning "light, lamp". He was a Benjamite, the son of Jeuel and Maachah and the father of Kish the father of Saul (1 Chr 9:35-36).
Nadab: a Hebrew name, meaning "generous". He was a son of Jeuel, and his mother's name was Maachah. He was of the sons of Benjamin. He lived in Gibeon, and he was the head of his house (1 Chr 9:36).
And Gedor, and Ahio, and Zechariah, and Mikloth. [37]
Gedor: a Hebrew name, meaning "fortress or walled place". He was the son of Jeuel, and the brother of Ner and Kish, of the ancestors of Saul (1 Chr 9:35-37).
Mikloth: a Hebrew name, meaning "staff". It is the name of a Benjamite (1 Chr 9:37-38).
And Mikloth begat Shimeam.
And they also dwelt over against their brethren in Jerusalem, with their brethren. [38]
Shimeam: a Benjamite, he was the son of Mikloth, living in Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:38).
And Ner begat Kish; and Kish begat Saul; and Saul begat
Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Esh-baal. [39]
Jonathan: a Hebrew name, meaning "Jehovah has given".
Malchishua: a Hebrew name, meaning "the king is salvation".
Abinadat: a Hebrew name, meaning "the father is generous or delegated".
Esh-baal: a Hebrew name, meaning "man of Baal". It is the first name of Ishbosheth son of Saul (2 Sam 2:8).
And the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal: and Merib-baal begat Micah. [40]
Merib-baal: also called Mephibosheth, a Hebrew name meaning "removal of idols".
And the sons of Micah were, Pithon, and Melech, and Tahrea, and Ahaz. [41]
Melech: a Hebrew name, meaning "king". He was the son of Micah, grandson of Mephibosheth (1 Chr 9:41).
Tahrea: a Hebrew name, meaning "crafty". He was a man of the descendants of Saul through Jonathan (1 Chr 9:41).
Ahaz: a Hebrew name, meaning "he held," that is, "the Lord held". He was Ahaz son of Micah, of the descendants of Jonathan (1 Chr 9:42).
And Ahaz begat Jarah; and Jarah begat Alemeth, and Azmaveth, and Zimri;
and Zimri begat Moza; [42]
Jarah: a Hebrew name, meaning "honeycomb". He was a man of the descendants of Saul (1 Chr 9:42).

Azmaveth: a Hebrew name, meaning "death is strong". He was the son of Jehoadah, and one of the grandsons of Jehonathan son of Saul, and it is stated in (1 Chr 9:42) that this Azmaveth is the son of Jarah.
Zimri: a Hebrew name, perhaps meaning "he who resembles the wild ox", and he was a Benjamite of the descendants of Jonathan son of Saul (1 Chr 9:42).
Alemeth: a Hebrew name, meaning "concealment". He was the son of Jehoadah, of the sons of Benjamin. He was of the grandsons of King Saul (1 Chr 9:42).
And Moza begat Binea; and Rephaiah his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son. [43]
Moza: a Hebrew name, meaning "exit". It is the name of a man of the descendants of Saul (1 Chr 9:42-43).
Yina: this name appeared in the original and in most translations in the form "Binea". He was the son of Moza, of the descendants of Jonathan son of Saul (1 Chr 9:43).
Eleasah, Elasah: a Hebrew name meaning "God has made". It is the name of a man of the descendants of Saul and of his son Jonathan (1 Chr 9:43). His name appeared in the text in the form "Alasah".
And Azel had six sons, whose names are these:
Azrikam, Bocheru, then Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan:
these were the sons of Azel. [44]
Bocheru: a Hebrew name, meaning "firstborn". He was a son of Azel (1 Chr 9:44).
Ishmael: a Hebrew name, meaning "God hears". He was a Benjamite called Ishmael son of Azel (1 Chr 9:44).
Sheariah: a Hebrew name, meaning "power of Jehovah". A man of the descendants of Saul (1 Chr 9:44).
Hanan: a Hebrew name, meaning "gracious, compassionate, generous". He was a son of Azel, of the descendants of Jonathan son of Saul (1 Chr 9:44).
My heart and my flesh cry out for the living God
v My God, my sins and the sins of my fathers have spoiled the joy of the Spirit in the community as in my heart.
By returning to You and cleaving to Your word, You restore to me more than I had lost, and You bring me and my brethren into the pledge of heaven.
v Let me return from the captivity of sin to the Jerusalem above, and enjoy with my brethren union with You.
It does not concern me whether I am one of the people, or a priest or one of the Levite singers, or a keeper of the gates of Your holy house.
For all together become like a near-heavenly order.
Our hearts together with our bodies cry out to You, O living God.
You pour Your holiness upon all, O Sanctifier of all.
Your Holy Spirit works in all.
So that we bear the mark of faithfulness and sincerity!
Truly we become members of Your body, O Son of David!

entries.section: 1. The killing of the sons of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: 1 Now the Philistines fought against Israel; and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines, and fell down slain in mount Gilboa. 2 And the Philistines followed hard after Saul, and after his sons; and the Philistines slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul.
Now the Philistines fought against Israel; and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines, and fell down slain in mount Gilboa. [1]

entries.section: 1. The killing of the sons of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: After reviewing the genealogies, or the history of the children of Israel from creation to the Babylonian captivity (586 B.C.) in the preceding chapters, the writer returned to the period when the kingdom of Israel began. He did not begin with Saul’s receiving the kingship, but with his death, in order to bring us to the age of David, as the king whom God had chosen, who received a promise that his seed would reign forever. This was fulfilled by the coming of the King of kings, the Son of David, who reigns over our hearts eternally and raises up from His Church the Queen who sits at His right hand. Josephus, the Jewish historian, comments on what is said in this chapter [2], saying that since the writer opens his account of Saul the king with this battle, it is as though he wished to say that there was nothing good in the life of Saul worth mentioning on his behalf. He reigned for twenty years, as it were, without good fruit, and his life ended by his own hands, but with God’s permission, as though the Lord had killed him [14].

This period was one of the worst in the life of Israel, for the people insisted on appointing a king, which grieved the heart of Samuel the prophet (1 Sam 8:6). Although victories were achieved over some of the nations, the king sinned, and instead of repenting of his sins, what concerned him was his personal honor before the people. So his life ended with the people falling, together with their king, before the Philistines. It is as though the outcome of the people’s insistence on appointing a king like the other nations, and of Saul’s insistence on his own honor, was destruction for the king and the people!

entries.section: 1. The killing of the sons of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: v What madness! Does this proud man not know that his glory vanishes and evaporates like a dream, and that greatness and authority are nothing but a deceptive mirage [3].

entries.section: 1. The killing of the sons of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: v The Pharisee prayed with himself and not with God, because the sin of pride turned him back to himself [4].

entries.section: 1. The killing of the sons of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: v He must not glorify himself nor utter anything that praises himself, nor find pleasure in listening to another’s praise of him, but serve in everything in secret, not working for the sake of appearance before men, but seeking the praise of God alone, and contemplating His glorious and awesome coming, as well as his own departure from this world, and the blessings prepared for the righteous and the fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Mt 25:41) [5].

St. Basil the Great What occupied the heart of the people was temporal things and not the Kingdom of God, so they received a king according to the desire of their hearts, a lover of temporal honor, and so he and his people lost both the temporal and the eternal.

entries.section: 1. The killing of the sons of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great sees that the work of the serpent, that is, Satan, is to corrupt our nature, so that we no longer look upward but bow down like the animals toward the dust, seeking earthly things. Therefore he advises us, saying: [The head of the beasts looks toward the earth, but the head of man was created to look toward heaven, and his eyes are directed upward. Therefore it is fitting for us to seek the things that are above, and with our insight to pierce through earthly things [6].]

entries.section: 1. The killing of the sons of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: And the Philistines followed hard after Saul, and after his sons; and the Philistines slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul. [2]
King Saul sinned, so disaster fell upon the people, and his sons also reaped the fruit of their father’s deeds.

Many are often astonished and ask: What fault is it of the people? And what crime have the sons committed? God allows this not in order to punish the people because of the sins of the leader, nor the sons because of the fathers, but in order to urge the people, as well as the sons, not to go astray after the errors of leaders and parents. This is what the Lord Christ affirms in saying: “He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Mt 10:37).

entries.section: 1. The killing of the sons of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: v The Holy Scripture commands us to obey our parents. Yes, but whoever loves them more than Christ loses his soul. Behold, the enemy (who persecutes me so that I may deny Christ) carries a sword to kill me; shall I then think of my mother’s tears? Or shall I despise the service of Christ for the sake of a father, whose burial I am not bound to attend if I am a servant of Christ (Lk 9:59-60), even though, as a true servant of Christ, I owe this (burial) to all [7].
St. Jerome

entries.section: 2. The suicide of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: 3 And the battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him, and he was wounded of the archers. 4 Then said Saul to his armourbearer, “Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and abuse me.” But his armourbearer would not; for he was sore afraid. So Saul took a sword, and fell upon it. 5 And when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise on the sword, and died. 6 So Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together. 7 And when all the men of Israel that were in the valley saw that they fled, and that Saul and his sons were dead, then they forsook their cities, and fled: and the Philistines came and dwelt in them.
And the battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him, and he was wounded of the archers. [3]

Saul abused the longsuffering of God, and thought that as a king possessing authority he was not subject to the law, and that there was no one to stand before him and call him to account. But divine justice overtook him and confronted him at the appropriate time, so his authority was taken from him, his family lost its dignity as a royal house, and David, the persecuted one, received the throne.

entries.section: 2. The suicide of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: v Many very negligent persons use God’s compassion as a pretext to increase the guilt of their sins, and carry their negligence to excess, saying thus: “There is no hell, there is no coming punishment. God forgives us all our sins.” To stop their mouths the wise man says: “Say not, His mercy is great; he will forgive the multitude of my sins” (Sir 5:6), and also: [As His mercy is great, so is His correction also] (Sir 16:12) [8].

entries.section: 2. The suicide of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: v Now if the laws of men are observed with care, how much more is this required for the laws of God. A man says: “But He is good.” How long shall we utter this folly? I say folly, not because God is not good, but because he thinks of His goodness in order to achieve this end... Listen to the Holy Scripture, which says: “Say not, His mercy is great; he will forgive the multitude of my sins” (Sir 5:6). He did not command us to say: “His mercy is great.” He does not enjoin us this, but rather He wants us to say this always, and with the following purpose, which the Apostle Paul raises with every kind of proof. He means: Do not marvel at the compassions of God so that you sin and say: “His mercy removes the multitude of my sins”... but rather that we may not despair because of our sins, but repent, for “the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance” (Rom 2:4), not to a greater evil [9].

entries.section: 2. The suicide of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom v (The Lord) says through the mouth of the prophet: [My son, add not sin unto sin and say, The mercy of God is great] (Sir 5:5-6). “Not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance” (Rom 2:4). For who is as merciful as God, who forgives all the sins of those who return to Him, and makes the wild olive tree a partaker of the fatness of the olive tree; and likewise who is as strict as He, so that He breaks off the natural branches because of their unbelief? (Rom 11:17-24) [10].

St. Augustine More than once Saul aimed his spear at David to kill him, but the spear did not reach David, because the Lord preserved him for the purity of his heart. But as for King Saul, when one of the soldiers aimed his spear at him, he struck him at once with a serious wound, as though he drank from the cup that he had filled to give David to drink.

entries.section: 2. The suicide of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: Then said Saul to his armourbearer,
“Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and abuse me.”
But his armourbearer would not; for he was sore afraid.
So Saul took a sword, and fell upon it. [4]
Here we notice the following in the situation of the wounded Saul:

A. Saul realized that the more he strove with all his effort to obtain temporal honor, the more, when he fell into the hands of the Philistines, he would receive bitter insults. Thus those who hold honors, or who love great honors, are exposed to the danger of being exposed to scandal and mockery.
B. Whoever does not give glory to God in his success, the unbelievers can dominate him and make a public spectacle of his corpse.

C. Since Saul disobeyed the divine commandment more than once, even in the moments of his death he asked his armourbearer to draw his sword and kill him, so that the enemy would not mock him, but he did not listen to him; rather he disobeyed him.

entries.section: 2. The suicide of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: And when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise on the sword, and died. [5]

entries.section: 2. The suicide of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: So Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together. [6]
Saul and his sons and all his house thought that they were a royal family with an inviolability that no one could touch, but behold, they fell under judgment in a single day, all at once.

entries.section: 2. The suicide of Saul on Mount Gilboa

paragraphs.text: And when all the men of Israel that were in the valley saw that they fled, and that Saul and his sons were dead, then they forsook their cities, and fled: and the Philistines came and dwelt in them. [7]
By faith Israel enjoyed the Promised Land in a spirit of victory, strength and success, but through sin they lost much, and destruction befell them.

entries.section: 3. The public disgrace and mockery of Saul and his sons

paragraphs.text: 8 And it came to pass on the morrow, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, that they found Saul and his sons fallen in mount Gilboa. 9 And when they had stripped him, they took his head, and his armour, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about, to carry tidings unto their idols, and to the people. 10 And they put his armour in the house of their gods, and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.
And it came to pass on the morrow, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, that they found Saul and his sons fallen in mount Gilboa. [8]

entries.section: 3. The public disgrace and mockery of Saul and his sons

paragraphs.text: And when they had stripped him, they took his head, and his armour, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about, to carry tidings unto their idols, and to the people. [9]

entries.section: 3. The public disgrace and mockery of Saul and his sons

paragraphs.text: The Hindus practice such a custom: when they triumph over their enemies they carry the good news to their idols with a great celebration and procession [11].

entries.section: 3. The public disgrace and mockery of Saul and his sons

paragraphs.text: And they put his armour in the house of their gods, and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon. [10]

Dagon: one of the most important gods of the Philistines, whom they believed to be the god who sends the rain and supplies them with abundant crops. Therefore they built temples for him wherever they settled in a land in Canaan where grain is grown. When drought came they cried out to him to send them rain. And if distress became severe they offered their children to him as sacrifices to appease him, and they used the temples to humiliate captives and to make a public spectacle of them by every means, as a kind of entertainment and glorification of Dagon (Judg 16:23-30), reckoning in this an honoring of the idols and an acknowledgment of their power.

entries.section: 4. The men of Jabesh-gilead bury the bones of Saul and his sons

paragraphs.text: And when all Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, [11]

entries.section: 4. The men of Jabesh-gilead bury the bones of Saul and his sons

paragraphs.text: They arose, all the valiant men, and took away the body of Saul, and the bodies of his sons, and brought them to Jabesh, and buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh, and fasted seven days. [12]
The valiant men of Jabesh-gilead had not forgotten that Saul had earlier rescued their city (1 Sam 11), so they wished to repay his good deed after his death.

Although God had permitted the chastening of Saul even in the manner of his death, He permitted the heroes of Jabesh-gilead to take the bodies of Saul and his sons and carry them to Jabesh. For despite the faults and evils of Saul and his sons, they felt bound to honor him and his sons as their leaders even after their death and the abuse done to them. So it is fitting for the believer to give honor to whom honor is due, whether in the Church, at work, in the state, or in the army (1 Thess 5:12-13; Rom 13:1-7).
Likewise David the prophet bore no feelings of revenge or gloating toward Saul, who bore bitter enmity toward him without cause.

13 So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD, even against the word of the LORD, which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; 14 And enquired not of the LORD: therefore he slew him, and turned the kingdom unto David the son of Jesse.
So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD, even against the word of the LORD, which he kept not.
And also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; [13]

He gave two reasons for his death. First, Saul sinned by his disobedience to the Lord. He did not keep the word of the Lord (1 Sam 13; 15). Saul was condemned for his lack of faithfulness to the word of the Lord. This ingratitude, sadly, was the mark of all the kings of Israel (the northern kingdom) and some of the kings of Judah.

Second: by his turning to the familiar spirit to seek counsel instead of turning to God (1 Sam 28). The writer considers that Saul’s resort to divination, rather than turning to God, corrupted every aspect of his life.
And enquired not of the LORD: therefore he slew him, and turned the kingdom unto David the son of Jesse. [14]
Saul had earlier sought God’s guidance (1 Sam 28:5-6), but here he did not seek His guidance.

This contradiction reveals what was in Saul’s heart. Although he had earlier sought God’s guidance, it was when he had no other means before him. And perhaps when he sought God he did so in a deadly literalism, without trust in God or true reliance. For Saul was known for his selfishness, seeking his own personal glory and popularity and not the glory of God, and he was marked by a spirit of stubbornness and constant rebellion.

David was given many opportunities to be rid of Saul (1 Sam 31:3-4), but he did not stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed, despite God’s promise to him of receiving the throne; and when Saul died he wept for him and lamented him with all love and sincerity, without haste to take up the rule.

David did not hasten to seize the throne, although he knew that God had rejected Saul and had chosen him as king. In patience and expectation of the work of God, and in complete surrender into His hands, he did not hasten events, so that he might receive the throne from the hand of God at the appropriate time.

“Therefore he slew him,” although it was he himself who put an end to his own life (1 Sam 31:3-4). Because of his continual stubbornness and rebellion (1 Sam 15:22-23), the grace of God forsook him and left him to carry out his evil will, so he killed himself by his own will.

entries.section: The death of Saul and the rising of the new man

paragraphs.text: The end of King Saul represents the old carnal man, who must die, and King David takes his place, representing the new spiritual man who is in the image of his Creator. As the Apostle Paul says: “That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; and be renewed in the spirit of your mind; and that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness” (Eph 4:22-24).

v [The king’s daughter is all glorious within] (Ps 45:13)... The man who joins himself to the love of the Father who sees in secret (Mt 6:6), and prays and works without his aim being the glory of men but the glory of God (Mt 6:10), is like the king’s daughter, all his glory being within. Do not look for garments fitting for one who is in the image of the Creator, as the Apostle says: “Seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds; and have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him” (Col 3:9-10), “Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering” (Col 3:12). Such a man is adorned from within, in his inner man. The Apostle also urges us [to put on the Lord Jesus Christ] (Rom 13:14), not in our outward man, but so that the thought of God may wholly take control of our thought. But I believe that the woven spiritual garments are woven by the building word, especially if it is accompanied by positive work. Also, just as garments are woven on a loom, in which the threads are interlaced, so it is with the word accompanied by positive work; it resembles the holy garment of the soul that is filled with sayings of virtue and the doing of them [12].

v [Sing unto the Lord a new song; play skilfully on the harp to honor Him] (Ps 33:3). Sing unto the Lord a truly new song, that is, worship the Lord, [not in the oldness of the letter, but in newness of spirit] (Rom 7:6).

The man who does not understand the Law in a literal way, but grasps it with a spiritual understanding, is able to sing a new song, for the Old Testament has grown old and passed away, and the new song, renewed by the teachings of the Lord, has appeared to us. He is the one who renews our youth like the eagle’s (Ps 103:5), “though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Cor 4:16), and the one who [reaches forth unto those things which are before] (Phil 3:13) is renewed more and more. And the one who is renewed prays to God always a truly new song.

Truly the expression “new” is applied to something exceptional and recent. When you describe the Incarnation of the Lord, which surpasses all nature, you are singing a new and unusual song. And when you explain the birth of the world and its complete renewal, after it had grown old through sin, the new birth that renewed it with a thorough renewal, you are singing a truly new song. Likewise when you speak of the Resurrection, you are singing a truly new and recent song [13].
St. Basil the Great
Let my old man die, and let my new man rise in Your image!
v In the waters of Baptism You crucified my old man with all his lusts.
And You granted me the new man who is in Your image.
Grant me that with every day my old man may be crucified with all his deeds.
Make sin bitter in my mouth, so that I may not desire it nor be enslaved to it.
With every morning let me cling to You the more, that Your splendor may shine upon my mind, my heart and all my senses.
Let me be counted in truth a member of Your body, O Son of David.
v Let Saul die, and his sons and all the people of his house.
May You shatter all corruption within me, and let David live and reign in my heart.
You establish Your Kingdom within me, so that I enjoy royal authority even over my thoughts.
You remove from me all that is foreign to You.
And You grant me to become in truth Your holy Jerusalem.
v Come, O Son of David and his Lord, and reveal Your glory within me!
Then my depths will become a new heaven, into which no corruption or sin will creep.
But it will be renewed with every morning, and my soul will rejoice in You!
Appendix 1 Chr 10

entries.section: 1. The crowning of David, the man of God, as king

paragraphs.text: 1 Then all Israel gathered themselves to David unto Hebron, saying, “Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh. 2 And moreover in time past, even when Saul was king, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel: and the LORD thy God said unto thee, Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be ruler over my people Israel.” 3 Therefore came all the elders of Israel to the king to Hebron; and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD; and they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD by Samuel.

What is recorded in this chapter is taken from Second Samuel. What is said in [1-9] reflects what is recorded in (2 Sam 5:1-10); and [10-47] what is recorded in (2 Sam 23:8-39). The writer ignored everything recorded in the first four chapters of Second Samuel. He did not refer to the short reign of Ish-bosheth, nor to the troubles of Abner, nor to Joab’s stretching out his hand to kill Abner. Rather the writer went directly to the gathering of the tribes together at Hebron, David’s first capital before his capture of Jerusalem, in order to make him king. Here he brought out all Israel in a single unity.

The Second Book of Samuel presents to us in some detail how David the prophet reached the royal throne, whereas the Book of Chronicles is content to affirm that it was God who brought David to the throne, using many people, even some from the tribe of Benjamin, the brethren of Saul.
God is the Controller of history; He turns all things to the building up of His people, without compelling anyone to move by force.

Truly it seemed that many tried to hinder the work of God and His plan for His believers, but God turns even evil into good, as happened with Joseph the son of Jacob: his brothers intended evil against him, and the Lord wrought good for him through their evil.
Then all Israel gathered themselves to David unto Hebron, saying,
“Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh. [1]
This book does not refer to the installation of David as king over Judah in Hebron; rather it begins with the gathering of all the tribes and their making him king over all.

The Book of Samuel recorded this period of history, and mentioned that David reigned for seven and a half years over the south, that is Judah, and that his capital was Hebron. This is not mentioned in Chronicles, because God looks upon Israel as one nation made up of twelve tribes; so from the standpoint of divine inspiration David became king over the twelve tribes.

The appointment of David as king was accomplished on the basis of the following: 1. His relationship with them, for they said to him: “Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh” [1]. They boasted of their attachment to him. They came to him because they were of his bone and his flesh. But the Son of David came down to us, and made us of His flesh and His bones. The Apostle says: “For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones” (Eph 5:30). The Lord Christ gave Himself as an example, for in His union with the Church, the Bride, as St. Augustine says, He left the Father, in that He emptied Himself of the glories and took the form of a servant (Phil 2:7), though He remained one with Him in essence without separation. He also left His mother, that is the Jewish people from whom He took the body through St. Mary, Jewish by race, that He might become one flesh with His Bride [1]. 2. Because of his conduct, especially that he did not stretch out his hand against Saul, who spared no effort to be rid of him. His love for his opponents drew them to him. St. Augustine says in his address to those preparing for the sacrament of Baptism: [Love alone is the distinguishing mark between the children of God and the children of the devil. Let us mark ourselves with the sign of the cross of Jesus Christ... and let us all be baptized. And let all come to the Church that we may build the walls of the Church, for there is nothing that distinguishes the children of God from the children of the devil except love.] 3. This was not accomplished by human strength, but according to the word of the Lord by Samuel. Samuel had earlier anointed him king at the command of the Lord (1 Sam 16:13), and now he was anointed a second time.

entries.section: 1. The crowning of David, the man of God, as king

paragraphs.text: And moreover in time past, even when Saul was king, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel: and the LORD thy God said unto thee,
Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be ruler over my people Israel.” [2]
The command was issued by the Lord Himself: the LORD thy God said unto thee that thou shalt feed my people Israel [2].

David, as king, occupied their hearts before he received the throne, even when Saul was king [2]. It was not the seat that made David king, but God made him king while he was a boy, before he sat on the throne!

What is recorded in this book in general, and in this chapter in particular, completes what is said of David the king in the books of Samuel and Kings. Perhaps David stood out in those books as a man of faith, with strength of personality, courage and works that were exceptional through the Lord. But what this book presents is that David is a godly man who loves the worship of the living temple.
In the earlier books we see David the saint and the sinner, yet faithful in consecrating his heart and all his depths to God.
In reality the two portraits of David’s character in the earlier books and in this book are not contradictory, but are one complete portrait.
The book does not refer here to the short and failed reign of Ishbosheth (2 Sam 2-4), but passes directly to the crowning of David as king.

The Second Book of Samuel has already given us many details concerning David’s attainment of power, where God uses the efforts of many people, some of them from Saul’s family; but what is affirmed here is that God is the One who directs events, accomplishing everything as He wills.
Saul tried to destroy or hinder the plan for David’s receiving power, but God is the Controller of history and the One who cares for His people, and He seated David as king at the appropriate time.

entries.section: 1. The crowning of David, the man of God, as king

paragraphs.text: Therefore came all the elders of Israel to the king to Hebron; and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the LORD; and they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD by Samuel. [3]
All the elders of Israel gathered to King David in Hebron, and he made a covenant with them before the Lord.

Here he affirms that David’s ascent to the throne was not by chance, nor the fruit of David’s nobility and ability, but according to God’s plan and grace, and it is bound up with a divine promise declared to David while he was still a boy tending his father’s sheep.

David reigned over Judah seven and a half years before he reigned over all Israel and took Jerusalem, and twenty years after Samuel anointed him king (1 Sam 16:1-13). For everything with God has its appointed time.

The divine promise was fulfilled despite the difficulties that David faced, until the promise seemed impossible. Perhaps some thought that the mercies of God had forsaken him, but at the appropriate time they appeared. David’s troubles were by God’s permission, that he might truly experience God’s love, care and wisdom.

entries.section: 2. The need for Jerusalem as a capital

paragraphs.text: 4 And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, which is Jebus; where the Jebusites were, the inhabitants of the land. 5 And the inhabitants of Jebus said to David, “Thou shalt not come hither.” Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion, which is the city of David. 6 And David said, “Whosoever smiteth the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain.” So Joab the son of Zeruiah went first up, and was chief. 7 And David dwelt in the castle; therefore they called it the city of David. 8 And he built the city round about, even from Millo round about: and Joab repaired the rest of the city. 9 So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him.
Since all the tribes together enjoyed David as king, the need became pressing for a capital worthy of this nation.

The capture of Jerusalem and its establishment as the capital was a wise move by David and his men. For Jerusalem is close to the border between the southern tribes and the northern tribes, and it is considered an effective factor in uniting the tribes together, without arousing feelings of envy and jealousy among them. It can rightly be said that Jerusalem was the heart and center of the people, and it was the fitting place to set up a temple for the Lord, representing the divine presence in the midst of all the people [2].

Its population in the days of David’s reign was about two thousand; the number rose to five thousand in the days of Solomon, and to seven thousand before the captivity, and most likely fell to less than five thousand in the days when the book was written. And before the destruction of the second temple in A.D. 70 the number was more than 80 thousand [3]. Through the vicissitudes of history, this city that David established as a capital has remained the heart of Judea.
And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem (which is Jebus).
And the Jebusites were there, the inhabitants of the land. [4]

Much is said about Jerusalem in the Holy Bible, and the holy city took its name from the Salem of Melchizedek, and from the name of Mount Moriah where Abraham offered his son Isaac, for “Jehovah-jireh” is the name that Abraham gave to Mount Moriah (Gen 22:14), and the temple was built in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah.

entries.section: 2. The need for Jerusalem as a capital

paragraphs.text: The following verses speak of David’s building around Jerusalem; he took the castle of Zion, which had been in the hands of the Jebusites until then, and called it the city of David [7], and verse (6) of Psalm (2) (Ps 2:6) refers to this: “As for me, I have anointed my king on Zion, my holy mountain”; for the city of David is in reality the region of Mount Zion.

David chose Jerusalem as the capital of the kingdom for political and military reasons. Because it lay to a large extent between the borders of the tribes, near the center of the kingdom, its location was neutral, reducing the tribes’ jealousy of one another. It was also on a high mountain, which made attacking it difficult.

The Jebusites did not expect that any force could storm them, because of the impregnable walls of Jerusalem and its being surrounded by strong rocks. They reckoned that they were safe, and did not realize that God is the Rock who preserves His children, and the refuge of those who trust in Him.

David and all the men of Israel set out from Hebron to Jerusalem, which was called Jebus, and the Jebusites were dwelling there, and they refused the entry of David and his men. And just as David and his men dwelt in Jebus, which became “Jerusalem,” that is, the city of peace, so we dwell with the Son of David and the place is transformed into a new Jerusalem. St. Gregory of Nazianzus sees that Jerusalem is our new inheritance.

v Farewell, for our massive and renewed temple has become our inheritance, and the secret of its greatness is the Word (Jesus Christ); for it was once called “Jebus,” and now we have made it Jerusalem [4].
St. Gregory of Nazianzus Jerusalem has become a symbol of heaven, as of the heart of the believer as the second heaven, for it is said:

“Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name” (Rev 3:12)
“I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev 21:2)
“And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain, and shewed me that great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God” (Rev 21:10)

v Some define a city as a gathering of beings in one organized body, governed by law... This definition given to the city suits the Jerusalem above... the heavenly city, because there is the church of the firstborn, whose names are written in the heavens (Heb 12:23). For it is also organized, since the flow of the life of the saints never ceases and it is governed by the heavenly law. Human nature cannot comprehend the extent of the readiness and order of this city, for [Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him] (1 Cor 2:9). Also in this city there are myriads of angels... and the church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven (Heb 12:22-23)... David mentions this city and says: Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God (Ps 87:3). What God promised to this city Isaiah conveys to us: [I will make thee an eternal excellency.. a joy... of many generations] Violence shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy borders; but thou shalt call thy walls Salvation (Isa 60:15-18). Let us lift up the eyes of our souls, and let us seek the higher good things that befit the city of God [5].

v Sheep are earthly and bowed down to the earth, but man is a heavenly being, who rises above them both by the structure of his body and by the dignity of his spirit. What is the form of the animals that go on four feet? Their head is bowed down to the earth, and they look at their belly, and only follow the needs of their belly. But your head, O man, is raised toward heaven, and your eyes look upward; yet you descend through the passions of the flesh, and become a slave to your belly and its lusts. So you reach the level of the animals for no reason, and become like them. You are called to things more noble: “Seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God” (Col 3:1). Lift yourself above the world... make your conversation in heaven. For your true homeland is the heavenly Jerusalem, and your countrymen are “the church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven (Heb 12:23) [6].
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: 2. The need for Jerusalem as a capital

paragraphs.text: And the inhabitants of Jebus said to David,
“Thou shalt not come hither.”
Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion (which is the city of David). [5]
It tells us of David’s capture of Jebus, or Jerusalem, and that it was called the city of David [4-9].
St. Jerome presents to us a spiritual meaning of the castle of Zion, or the fortress of Zion, in which we take refuge against those who come against us.

entries.section: 2. The need for Jerusalem as a capital

paragraphs.text: v You have great shrewdness and an inexhaustible store of language; your style is smooth and pure, and your eloquence and purity are mingled with wisdom. Your head is good and all your senses are kindled with intelligence. Add to this wisdom and eloquence earnest study and knowledge of the Holy Scripture. Then I shall soon see you in your fortress against all who come against you. You will go up with Joab on the roof of Zion and sing on the housetops what you have learned in the secret chambers [7].
St. Jerome

entries.section: 2. The need for Jerusalem as a capital

paragraphs.text: And David said, “Whosoever smiteth the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain.”
So Joab the son of Zeruiah went first up, and was chief. [6]
Here alone among the other books it makes clear how Joab became the commander of David’s army [6-7], and it declared that Joab built the city and repaired it [8].

Joab, of whom the Book of Samuel does not speak, occupies the first place after David. We do not see him here as the ambitious and spiteful man, but as the one appointed according to God’s plan to overcome the castle of Zion for David the king. It is said of him that he smote the Jebusites and so became chief, and that he repaired a part of the city.

This book does not refer to Joab’s conflict with Abner and his revenge on this noble commander, just as it is silent about David’s sorrowful words: “And I am this day weak, though anointed king; and these men the sons of Zeruiah be too hard for me: the LORD shall reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness” (2 Sam 3:39).

entries.section: 2. The need for Jerusalem as a capital

paragraphs.text: This book did not criticize Joab but revealed everything positive in the life of Joab, and did not refer to David’s curse upon him (1 Kgs 2:5), and ignores what is negative in his life. What the book affirms is that God’s plan concerning David is being fulfilled, and that Joab and others are instruments for that [10].

entries.section: 2. The need for Jerusalem as a capital

paragraphs.text: And David dwelt in the castle; therefore they called it the city of David. [7]

entries.section: 2. The need for Jerusalem as a capital

paragraphs.text: And he built the city round about, even from Millo round about:
and Joab repaired the rest of the city. [8]
The writer ascribes to David the building of the walls, and to Joab the building of the houses, which is a work of little importance compared with the walls.

entries.section: 2. The need for Jerusalem as a capital

paragraphs.text: So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him [9]
The secret of David’s strength is the Lord, for it is said of him: “So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him” [9].

Saul used his strength and abilities for the sake of himself, his lust, his popularity and his authority, and so he collapsed; while David sought to enjoy the divine presence, so his stature increased, for the Almighty was with him. The secret of David’s success was his reliance on God, and the secret of Saul’s decline was his self-regard, ignoring God (1 Sam 15:17-26). What occupied David was the glory of God and his attachment to Him; therefore God lifted him from glory to glory.

St. Augustine sees in this expression the harmony between the free will that God gives to man and the divine work in the life of His believers, to give them the will, the word and the work. Thus we do not ignore David’s role in his success, but it is not accomplished without the grace of God, which gave him a holy will and the ability to work according to God’s will.
v Without doubt human wills cannot resist the will of God, who does whatever pleases Him in heaven and on earth (Isa 45:11).
The human will cannot prevent Him from doing what He wills, seeing that even by human wills He does what He wills, when He wills to do this...
Such was the case of David, whom God established over the kingdom with a joyful result.

We read of him: “So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him” [9]. A little later it is said: “Then the spirit came upon Amasai, who was chief of the thirty (the captains), and he said, Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse: peace, peace be unto thee, and peace be to thine helpers; for thy God helpeth thee” (1 Chr 12:18).
