Could Amasai have opposed the will of God, even though he was fulfilling His will, seeing that God, through His Spirit with whom Amasai was clothed, worked in his heart that he should will thus, speak thus, and act thus?
In the same way, a little after that, the Scripture says: [All these men of war, that could keep rank, came with a perfect heart to Hebron, to make David king over all Israel] (1 Chr 12:38).

It is clear that by their own will they made David king; this fact is plain and cannot be denied. And yet it is God who works in human hearts as He wills, who wills and works this will in them. This is the reason for which the Scripture said first: “So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him” [9].

The Lord God who was with David brought these men to make him king. How did He make them so? Certainly not by binding them with any material chains. Rather He worked in them and took hold of their hearts, and drew them by their own will which He created in them. Therefore when God wills to set up kings on the earth, He takes hold of the wills of the multitude by His power, more than by human power itself.
If this is so, certainly it is He, and not another, who gives useful counsels and makes adjustments in the heart of the one to whom He gives counsel, so that he may dwell in the heavenly kingdom [8].

St. Augustine again affirms that God does not compel a man to do the will of God by force, but when a man surrenders his life into the hand of God, God works that this man should will and act according to the will of God [9].

This chapter highlights the greatness of the character of David and of the heroes attached to him: 1. David a leader from the Lord: God chose David for the purity of his heart and his faithfulness in little, that is, in tending his father’s sheep. Now all the men of Israel choose him, because they perceived how the Lord was with him, whereas Saul, though he was made king, was not faithful to the Lord. 2. David supports Joab to be a leader: David had his role in supporting Joab and in his taking up the leadership work. David was a capable leader, but he could not accomplish everything by himself. The successful leader raises up successful and faithful leaders who work with him. 3. Heroes glorified in a simple deed: Joab did a great deed, in that he smote the Jebusites [6]. But these three did not disdain to perform a simple deed, in bringing water from the well of Beth-lehem, that was at the gate [18]. Often the greatness of some shows in the practice of small things. 4. The great fall in matters in which the weak may not fall, such as David’s killing of Uriah the Hittite [41] in order to take his wife.

entries.section: 3. A leader who raises up leaders

paragraphs.text: 10 These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel. 11 And this is the number of the mighty men whom David had; Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains: he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time. 12 And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite, who was one of the three mighties. 13 He was with David at Pasdammim, and there the Philistines were gathered together to battle, where was a parcel of ground full of barley; and the people fled from before the Philistines. 14 And they set themselves in the midst of that parcel, and delivered it, and slew the Philistines; and the LORD saved them by a great deliverance. 15 Now three of the thirty captains went down to the rock to David, into the cave of Adullam; and the host of the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim. 16 And David was then in the hold, and the Philistines’ garrison was then at Beth-lehem. 17 And David longed, and said, “Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Beth-lehem, that is at the gate!” 18 And the three brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Beth-lehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David: but David would not drink of it, but poured it out to the LORD, 19 And said, “My God forbid it me, that I should do this thing: shall I drink the blood of these men that have put their lives in jeopardy? for with the jeopardy of their lives they brought it.” Therefore he would not drink it. These things did these three mightiest. 20 And Abishai the brother of Joab, he was chief of the three: for lifting up his spear against three hundred, he slew them, and had a name among the three. 21 Of the three, he was more honourable than the two; for he was their captain: howbeit he attained not to the first three. 22 Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts; he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day. 23 And he slew an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits high; and in the Egyptian’s hand was a spear like a weaver’s beam; and he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and slew him with his own spear. 24 These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and had the name among the three mighties. 25 Behold, he was honourable among the thirty, but attained not to the first three: and David made him one of his confidants. 26 Also the valiant men of the armies were, Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Beth-lehem, 27 Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite, 28 Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Antothite, 29 Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite, 30 Maharai the Netophathite, Heled the son of Baanah the Netophathite, 31 Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah, that pertained to the children of Benjamin, Benaiah the Pirathonite, 32 Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite, 33 Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, 34 The sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shage the Hararite, 35 Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur, 36 Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite, 37 Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai the son of Ezbai, 38 Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Haggeri, 39 Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Berothite, the armourbearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, 40 Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite, 41 Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai, 42 Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a captain of the Reubenites, and thirty with him, 43 Hanan the son of Maachah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite, 44 Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel the sons of Hothan the Aroerite, 45 Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite, 46 Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite, 47 Eliel, and Obed, and Jasiel the Mesobaite.

The successful leader supports many, that they may become leaders: 1. Joab the head: he said: [Whosoever smiteth the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain] [6]. Joab succeeded as chief of David’s warriors. 2. Three leaders [11-19]: David longed to drink water from the well of Beth-lehem that was at the gate [17]. What is this well but the work of the Holy Spirit in the Incarnation of the Word in Beth-lehem, which opened the gates of heaven? David did not drink the water, but offered it as a libation to the Lord; what he asks of leaders is for the sake of the Lord [18]. 3. Three other leaders, headed by Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, who slew two lionlike men of Moab and a lion in a pit in a snowy day [22], and killed the Egyptian giant with a staff [23]. The lion signifies the devil (1 Pet 5:8), and the Egyptian giant the love of the world. 4. The valiant men of the armies [26-47]: some of them were by birth enemies of Israel, from nations that opposed Israel, who became servants for the sake of the Kingdom of God. Among these: Zelek the Ammonite [39], Ithmah the Moabite [46], and Uriah the Hittite [41].

entries.section: 3. A leader who raises up leaders

paragraphs.text: It is clear that David’s character, with its godliness together with its courage and sincerity, drew many men of valor and military leaders to work with him. 1. This chapter presents to us Joab as chief of David’s warriors. 2. The chapter referred to a group called the “three” [11] who seem to have had a special standing as heroes. 3. After them came the group of “the thirty,” who are the most prominent figures among David’s warriors in his early days, previously mentioned in (2 Sam 23:24-39); most of them from the house of David and some from the other tribes. 4. The number increased with those coming from the other tribes as a result of his growing popularity, so the book added 16 persons to the list of the thirty, perhaps to confirm the growth of David’s popularity.

The list of the army chiefs was set down at the beginning of his reign. In (2 Sam 23) we find a similar list set down at the end of his reign. A few names that appear in Samuel do not appear here, but a large number has been added. The chapter refers to 81 mighty men, 20 of whom are mentioned without their names being given, while in Samuel (chapter 23) 37 of them are mentioned. In Second Samuel the mighty men are mentioned as supporters of David in establishing his throne. But here it is to recognize God’s plan and His work in establishing the throne for His anointed.
These mighty men came to David at different times. Some came when he was in the cave of Adullam [15-19], some when he was in Ziklag (1 Chr 12:1-22), and others when he was in Hebron (1 Chr 12:23-40).

These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel. [10]

Divine inspiration affirmed that the secret of the increase of David’s greatness is that the LORD of hosts was with him [9], and immediately it began to speak of the chief of the mighty men whom he had.

When the believer is in fellowship with the LORD of hosts, his success is not confined to his own personal growth, but extends also to those who work with him. It is not fitting for the great to ascribe their greatness to themselves in arrogance and pride, but to God who works in them and in those who work with them.

God works through us and in us by His grace, which also works in those who work with us! The sign of being with God is that He works through all; for God is all in all, and wills to work through everyone.
David strengthened himself with God, the God of hosts, and those who worked with him strengthened themselves with him, and all Israel strengthened themselves with them [10].

The work of God in the life of His people is that the faithful leader urges him to raise up leaders who grow in everything, and the leaders work on behalf of the whole community, and the community as a whole supports the king or the president or the leader. A wonderful fellowship between God and man, and between man and his fellow man.

The chief mighty men whom David had were those who followed him in the period of his rejection, and now that he has been raised to the throne, these also were raised, and here we find something necessary for our benefit.

David was a type of our Lord Jesus, who calls His believers His people, and they are [the mighty men whom He has]. At His coming the Lord Jesus was rejected by many. His own said: [We will not have this man to reign over us]. In these days of ours Christ is rejected by the world, so we are living in the period of the rejection of Christ, and He is calling His mighty men.
The following is a list of some of David’s men, mighty men of valor, and a few of their great deeds:
And this is the number of the mighty men whom David had;
Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains:
he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time. [11]
With his spear he killed three hundred at one time. God gave him a victory beyond nature over the enemies of his people.

entries.section: B. Eleazar the son of Dodo

paragraphs.text: 12 And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite, who was one of the three mighties. 13 He was with David at Pasdammim, and there the Philistines were gathered together to battle, where was a parcel of ground full of barley; and the people fled from before the Philistines. 14 And they set themselves in the midst of that parcel, and delivered it, and slew the Philistines; and the LORD saved them by a great deliverance.
And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite,
who was one of the three mighties. [12]
Eleazar the son of Dodo the Ahohite was faithful to David; he accompanied him even when the others forsook him.

entries.section: B. Eleazar the son of Dodo

paragraphs.text: He was with David at Pasdammim, and there the Philistines were gathered together to battle,
where was a parcel of ground full of barley; and the people fled from before the Philistines. [13]

All who were around David fled before the Philistines, but Eleazar stood firm in his place, therefore the Lord saved him. The most dangerous enemy of man is fear; but whoever stands firm with courage, trusting in God, enjoys victory.

entries.section: B. Eleazar the son of Dodo

paragraphs.text: And they set themselves in the midst of that parcel, and delivered it, and slew the Philistines;
and the LORD saved them by a great deliverance. [14]

All who were around Eleazar the son of Dodo fled before the Philistines, and he stood firm in his place, so the Lord saved him. He was a symbolic image of the Lord Christ in the midst of His sufferings, when He said: “Behold, the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (Jn 16:32).
When everyone forsakes a man, and he stands firm in God and does not waver, he enjoys victory.

If David and the heroes and all the people magnify themselves in God, the LORD of hosts, then all ought to strive not against men but against the powers of darkness (Eph 6:12), for the pagan Philistines signify evil and the powers of darkness. It is fitting for us to fight the good fight (2 Tim 4:7).

15 Now three of the thirty captains went down to the rock to David, into the cave of Adullam; and the host of the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim. 16 And David was then in the hold, and the Philistines’ garrison was then at Beth-lehem. 17 And David longed, and said, “Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Beth-lehem, that is at the gate!” 18 And the three brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Beth-lehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David: but David would not drink of it, but poured it out to the LORD, 19 And said, “My God forbid it me, that I should do this thing: shall I drink the blood of these men that have put their lives in jeopardy? for with the jeopardy of their lives they brought it.” Therefore he would not drink it. These things did these three mightiest.
Now three of the thirty captains went down to the rock to David, into the cave of Adullam; and the host of the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim. [15]
The story of the three heroes was preserved by the Book of Chronicles to reveal what was in David’s heart toward God and his intense concern for the life of his followers.

These thirty were the bravest and greatest leaders in David’s army. The three men who were set apart as the dearest of the heroes are those who brought David water from the well of Beth-lehem. This story carries a great symbolism, for David was brought up in Beth-lehem as his birthplace. And there was a well at its entrance; he would often return thirsty after tending the sheep and then drink from that well. And now he was besieged by the Philistines and could not go to that well, so he said: “Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Beth-lehem, that is at the gate!” It was merely a wish and was not a command, but the three brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Beth-lehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David. And the astonishing thing is that he would not drink it but poured it out as an offering to the LORD.

Here are similarities on which we can meditate. The Lord Jesus was born in Beth-lehem and He is this water from Beth-lehem; He is the water of life, and there are many mighty men through the generations and centuries who belong to Jesus Christ, who have brought this water to the thirsty world. And we notice that David’s men responded to the mere expression of a wish by him. For he could not give a command like this. And here is our Lord Jesus commanding us to take the water of life to the whole world; so what have we done with it? Are we obedient to His commands?

We also notice what David did with this water that was brought to him at great risk. David was not selfish, and it is no wonder that his men loved him and were ready to suffer for him, because he was ready to suffer with them. He did not drink the water, because his men had no water, and he preferred to be like them. The Psalm (1 Chr 22:14) tells us that at the death of our Lord Jesus Christ on the cross He said: “I am poured out like water”; He poured out His life like water on the earth, and took His place among us as one of us — taking what is ours to give us what is His — taking our body and giving us His Holy Spirit, and making us one with Him by His goodness [10].
And David was then in the hold, and the Philistines’ garrison was then at Beth-lehem. [16]
And David longed, and said,
“Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Beth-lehem, that is at the gate!” [17]
The water that David asked for from Beth-lehem signifies the Lord Christ, who was born in Beth-lehem.
v By the water that David the king desired, what did he long for, but the Son, who is the water of life for him who seeks Him?
Christ was called by the name of water, because he thirsted for Him, and it was known that He would come to the earth from Beth-lehem.
That seer (David) did not ask for water that issues from a spring, because the Son of God is not from marriage.
The water of the cistern comes from the top of the height, as Christ came down from on high, to become a drink.
The cistern is the Virgin, because the drink came down into her from on high, and no fountain rose up from the earth and poured the water into her.
The woman is also called a cistern in prophecy, and the man a mountain, and let him who reads understand [11].

St. Jacob of Serugh St. Augustine sees in the pouring out of the water as an offering a reference to the concept of fasting, that it is not a restraint or a shattering of the old passions, but replacing them with new and fitting joys.

v Keeping the Great Fast is not a restraint of the old passions, but an opportunity for new joys. Take into account, offering it with every possible diligence, that you prevent these situations from creeping up on you. The filling of the stomach must be blamed. Therefore the incentives to lust must be removed. For fasting is not a loathing of certain kinds of food, but a control of the fleshly lust... So the holy king David repented because of his excessive desire for water [12].
St. Augustine

And the three brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Beth-lehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David: but David would not drink of it, but poured it out to the LORD [18]

They risked their lives to bring water to David from the well of Beth-lehem. They did not do this to receive a word of praise, nor were their names mentioned. What concerned them was the joy of David’s heart.

It is fitting for us, when someone wishes to serve us or give us something for the sake of God who works in us, to offer this service or gift to God in the life of the needy. For what God gives us through them is a trust that we also offer to others, and He reckons it a gift offered to Himself personally.

He refused to drink the water, perhaps because he felt remorse that he had expressed his wish to drink from the well of Beth-lehem, since it was fitting for him to care for those around him, for they might have been more in need of water than he.
And said, “My God forbid it me, that I should do this thing:
shall I drink the blood of these men that have put their lives in jeopardy?
for with the jeopardy of their lives they brought it.”
Therefore he would not drink it.
These things did these three mightiest. [19]

These men risked their lives to please David, and they realized that their consecration to him came from their consecration to God, therefore he poured out the water as a drink offering, showing that God alone deserves such consecration. They offered the water to David, and he in turn offered it to God. For he reckoned that God alone deserves such consecration.
When we serve others for the sake of the Lord, we are serving God Himself.
St. John Chrysostom sees that those who share in the expenses of the preachers are reckoned as having contributed to the work of preaching.

entries.section: D. Abishai the brother of Joab

paragraphs.text: And Abishai the brother of Joab, he was chief of the three:
for lifting up his spear against three hundred, he slew them, and had a name among the three. [20]

entries.section: D. Abishai the brother of Joab

paragraphs.text: Of the three, he was more honourable than the two; for he was their captain: howbeit he attained not to the first three. [21]

Abshai (Abishai) the brother of Joab is considered the most honored of the three. The Holy Bible tells us that in his faithfulness to David he was steadfast without hesitation. He went with him to Saul’s camp (1 Sam 26), and accompanied him in his flight from Jerusalem when Absalom rebelled against him (2 Sam 16), and he it was who crushed the rebellion of Sheba (2 Sam 20), and delivered David from the giant Ishbi-benob (2 Sam 21). He rendered him services with all faithfulness (2 Sam 10; 18; 1 Chr 18).
Thus with courage, sincerity and self-sacrifice he served David; how much more is it fitting for us to serve the Lord of David, the King of kings?

entries.section: E. Benaiah the son of Jehoiada

paragraphs.text: 22 Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts; he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day. 23 And he slew an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits high; and in the Egyptian’s hand was a spear like a weaver’s beam; and he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and slew him with his own spear. 24 These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and had the name among the three mighties. 25 Behold, he was honourable among the thirty, but attained not to the first three: and David made him one of his confidants.
Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts;
he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day. [22]

The secret of the strength of these heroes is that the Lord who was with David was also with them. Joshua’s advice came: [Cleave unto the LORD your God, as ye have done unto this day. For the LORD hath driven out from before you great nations and strong: but as for you, no man hath been able to stand before you unto this day. One man of you shall chase a thousand: for the LORD your God, he it is that fighteth for you, as he hath promised you] (Josh 23:8-11).

entries.section: E. Benaiah the son of Jehoiada

paragraphs.text: And he slew an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits high; and in the Egyptian’s hand was a spear like a weaver’s beam;
and he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and slew him with his own spear. [23]
His father was a valiant priest (1 Chr 27:5).

He was chief over David’s guards. He took the place of Joab, the commander of the armies of Israel (1 Kgs 2:34-35). His victories present to us a picture of the life that is victorious over the world (Egypt), the flesh (Moab), and Satan (the prowling lion), for he overcame all these.

Zelek the Ammonite and Uriah the Hittite [39, 41] and Ithmah the Moabite [46] were by birth enemies of Israel, but they were transformed to become in the service of David, king of Israel.
We, as children of the fallen Adam, entered into enmity with God, but by grace we have become, in Christ Jesus, beloved children and good soldiers in the army of salvation.
Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Berothite, (the armourbearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah), [39]
Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite, [40]
Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai, [41]
The names mentioned in verses 41-47 do not appear in the list given in (2 Sam 23).

Among his faithful commanders was Uriah the Hittite [41], of a foreign race, who became faithful to him and a guard, but, sadly, he devised his killing (2 Sam 11) and married his wife. By repentance he rose from his fall, and submitted to the chastisements of God!

He was a member of the people whom the Israelites destroyed when they took possession of the Promised Land (Deut 7:1-2), yet we see him here as a warrior faithful to David. Sadly David sinned when he planned his killing in order to marry Bathsheba, his wife (2 Sam 11).
As for Uriah the Hittite, in Samuel he stands out as a witness to David’s sin. But here the book passes in silence over David’s hideous fall.
Nor is Eliam the son of Ahithophel mentioned (2 Sam 23:34), whose father was associated with treachery against David.

Teach me and train me in the spirit of leadership!
v Teach me, O Lord of hosts, how to acquire the spirit of leadership.
In Your love for mankind, You want everyone to be a leader.
You did not create a child to be a slave, but to be a king.
You delight in everyone who works through You in the spirit of leadership.
As long as You are with me, I walk in the spirit of confidence and certainty.
I ask that every human being be strengthened for You.
Then all will live in the spirit of defiance of the powers of darkness, as well as of suffering and even death.
v When shall we see Your people the one holy Bride in You?!
When shall we see her the striving Church who is crowned by You?!
She enters into Your embrace rejoicing.
The heavenly ones take pride in her, and rejoice in her victory.
v Grant us that each one may reckon his brother’s success as his own.
By Your love each one is strengthened, and all together are also strengthened!

1 Now these are they that came to David to Ziklag, while he yet kept himself close because of Saul the son of Kish: and they were among the mighty men, helpers of the war. 2 They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul’s brethren of Benjamin. 3 The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, the sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite; and Jeziel, and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; and Berachah, and Jehu the Antothite, 4 And Ismaiah the Gibeonite, a mighty man among the thirty, and over the thirty; and Jeremiah, and Jahaziel, and Johanan, and Josabad the Gederathite, 5 Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite, 6 Elkanah, and Jesiah, and Azareel, and Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korhites, 7 And Joelah, and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor.
Now these are they that came to David to Ziklag, while he yet kept himself close because of Saul the son of Kish: and they were among the mighty men, helpers of the war. [1]

David, full of love for his people, was deprived of finding a place for himself in his own country, and behold, Achish the Philistine king gave Ziklag to him and his family and those who gathered around him (1 Sam 27:5-7). He was happy that a famous warrior from among Israel should take refuge with him. David hid in Ziklag; but his movements were not completely secret.

From the historical side, in this period David is considered to have reached the extreme of weakness (see 1 Sam 27:1-7), but the Book of Chronicles here presents it as a brilliant period in the life of David, in which some members of the tribe of Benjamin (the brethren of Saul) went up to him. Men of mighty ability were drawn to David the outcast and gathered around him. The best of those who were in Saul’s army came to him. It is as though God was affirming to David that his enemies had become his men working with him [16].

They were marked by the following: 1. They were skilled in using arrows, bows, and stones with slings [1]. 2. They were marked by earnestness and strength of resolve, their faces like the faces of lions [8]. 3. Fit in body for wars, their swiftness like that of the gazelles on the mountains [8]. 4. Faithful to God and to the man of God [1-17].
Ziklag: a city in the south of Judah, first belonging to Simeon (Josh 19:5), then to the Philistines, and after that to Judah. David remained in Ziklag a year and four months until Saul died.

The wonderful thing is that these heroes, helpers in the war, among whom were the brethren of Saul, came to David in Ziklag and gathered around him without knowing that the time of Saul’s death had drawn near.

These heroes did not come to David after the death of Saul to flatter him, because they realized that the throne had come into David’s hands; rather they were drawn to him, saying through the mouth of Amasai: “for thy God helpeth thee” [18].
They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul’s brethren of Benjamin. [2]
The sling was humble in appearance, but deadly in battle, as the stone is hurled to its deadly target.
As for the bow and arrow, they had been used for thousands of years, and arrowheads were made of stone, wood or bones...
The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, the sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite; and Jeziel, and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; and Berachah, and Jehu the Antothite, [3]
And Ismaiah the Gibeonite, a mighty man among the thirty, and over the thirty; and Jeremiah, and Jahaziel, and Johanan, and Josabad the Gederathite [4]
Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite [5]
Elkanah, and Jesiah, and Azareel, and Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korhites [6]
And Joelah, and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor. [7]

entries.section: 2. The mighty men of Gad join David

paragraphs.text: 8 And of the Gadites there separated themselves unto David into the hold to the wilderness men of might, and men of war fit for the battle, that could handle shield and buckler, whose faces were like the faces of lions, and were as swift as the roes upon the mountains; 9 Ezer the first, Obadiah the second, Eliab the third, 10 Mishmannah the fourth, Jeremiah the fifth, 11 Attai the sixth, Eliel the seventh, 12 Johanan the eighth, Elzabad the ninth, 13 Jeremiah the tenth, Machbanai the eleventh. 14 These were of the sons of Gad, captains of the host: one of the least was over an hundred, and the greatest over a thousand. 15 These are they that went over Jordan in the first month, when it had overflown all his banks; and they put to flight all them of the valleys, both toward the east, and toward the west.

And of the Gadites there separated themselves unto David into the hold to the wilderness men of might, and men of war fit for the battle, that could handle shield and buckler, whose faces were like the faces of lions, and were as swift as the roes upon the mountains; [8]

Perhaps by “the hold” is meant the cave of Adullam (2 Sam 23:13). The Gadites deserve credit, because they shared with David while he was in distress. They also deserve credit in view of their strength and courage in war of every kind.

While the Benjamites were skilled in the use of bows and slings, the warriors from Gad were skilled in the use of shields and spears. Spearheads were made of bones or stones. As for the spears of the Philistines, their shafts were of bronze and their heads of iron, since they monopolized the manufacture of iron (1 Sam 13:19-20).

The book depicts for us the extent of the tribe of Gad’s conviction about making David king, for they separated themselves from their brethren on the east bank. It is a separation worthy of praise, because it rests on accepting David as king, although he was in the hold in the wilderness [8], perhaps one of the strong strongholds in En-gedi. Although the number mentioned here is small, eleven persons, yet they represented a force not to be despised, added to the force of David. They are heads of an army of heroes and brave men with the faces of strong lions and swiftness of movement like gazelles.
These did not come fleeing from distress, nor asking him for protection from an enemy, but they came convinced of him as the man of God appointed to be king over Israel.
These mighty men present to us a living example as good and faithful soldiers of Christ.

A. As these were heads of an army, so it is fitting for the believer to carry the spirit of strength, realizing that he has mighty abilities to resist sin and evil and corruption and the devil himself and all his wiles and deceits. He is a leader of all his energy and abilities in the Lord.

B. These had the faces of strong lions, not to carry a spirit of violence and predation, but to work in the spirit of strength for the sake of the Kingdom of God without fear. They are not troubled by affliction, and do not fear sickness or hardships or injustice. They say with the Psalmist: “For by thee I have run through a troop; and by my God have I leaped over a wall” (Ps 18:29). “Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident” (Ps 27:3).
They are marked by swiftness of movement, so that even on the mountains they hasten, not in fleeing before the enemy lest he overtake them, but they hasten in victory over the devil, their enemy.

entries.section: 2. The mighty men of Gad join David

paragraphs.text: Ezer the first, Obadiah the second, Eliab the third [9]

entries.section: 2. The mighty men of Gad join David

paragraphs.text: Mishmannah the fourth, Jeremiah the fifth [10]

entries.section: 2. The mighty men of Gad join David

paragraphs.text: Attai the sixth, Eliel the seventh [11]

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah the tenth, Machbanai the eleventh. [13]

entries.section: 2. The mighty men of Gad join David

paragraphs.text: These were of the sons of Gad, captains of the host.
One of the least was over an hundred, and the greatest over a thousand. [14]
What the Holy Bible affirms is that man was created as a leader who leads by the Holy Spirit of God all his senses and emotions and gifts, without servility or disturbance.
What occupies the believer’s heart is not the measure of his abilities to be head over a hundred or a thousand, but to be faithful in what is in his hands.

entries.section: 2. The mighty men of Gad join David

paragraphs.text: These are they that went over Jordan in the first month, when it had overflown all his banks; and they put to flight all them of the valleys, both toward the east, and toward the west. [15]
In the first month, that is in the month of Nisan, when the Jordan overflows all its banks (Josh 3:15).

As for the heroes of Benjamin, the brethren of Saul, the enmity of Saul their brother did not hinder them from acknowledging the kingship of David and supporting him. As for Gad, the obstacle was the location of their dwelling east of the Jordan, as though in a barrier from meeting David; yet although the river had filled its banks with water, they crossed the river with certainty, because their great love drew them to him.

Here is a group of men who came to David swimming in the Jordan at the time of flood, and they were about to lose heart when David came to meet them, and he did not know whether they were friends or enemies, so he said to them in effect: [If you have come to harm me I will destroy you], but they answered him: [Far be it, O David; we have come to be at your side]. For they wished to live for David and to be at his side to help him.

Many of us want to be in the service of the Lord, but think that it is merely a task to occupy time, but what matters is whether we want to live for Christ as these men wanted to live for David. And we can raise this meditation higher.

Christ brought us across the Jordan when we died and rose with Him in Holy Baptism, and He blessed us with every spiritual blessing, so we must serve Him not with the service of the lips or the wasting of time, but with complete submission to His will. We have crossed the Jordan not to serve David but to serve One who is greater than David.

By saying: “and they put to flight all them of the valleys, both toward the east, and toward the west,” it reveals the following: 1. They set out from the east of the Jordan and then crossed the river with strength and speed, then crossed in the west of the Jordan until they reached David.
This journey of theirs represents the journey of every believer who has come wishing to settle in the bosom of the Lord of David.

It is fitting for the believer to live as on the high mountains, not seeking the lowly and earthly things but the heavenly, and his heart does not settle in the valleys, that is, in the lowly passing things. He fights with the eastern and western things, that is, bodily pleasures and afflictions. His heart is not occupied with pleasures, and troubles and afflictions do not crush him. He walks in the way, passing over delights and troubles, pressing on to the things above. The Psalmist says: “The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies (a kind of rabbit)” (Ps 104:18).

v We have noticed indeed and truly that the wild goats signify the saints who came into this world in order to destroy the venom of the serpent. But let us see what are the high mountains that seem reserved for the wild goats alone, and which no one can climb who is not a wild goat. In my personal belief it is the knowledge of the Trinity that is called the high mountains, for no one reaches this knowledge unless he is a wild goat [5].

v Jesus Himself, when He was transfigured, this did not happen on the plain, but He went up on a mountain, and there He was transfigured. Understand from this that He always appears on the mountains or the hills, to teach you also, so do not seek Him in just any place, but on the mountains of the Law and the Prophets [6].
Origen

entries.section: 3. The children of Benjamin and Judah in the hold

paragraphs.text: 16 And there came of the children of Benjamin and Judah to the hold unto David. 17 And David went out to meet them, and answered and said unto them, “If ye be come peaceably unto me to help me, mine heart shall be knit unto you: but if ye be come to betray me to mine enemies, seeing there is no wrong in mine hands, the God of our fathers look thereon, and rebuke it.” 18 Then the spirit came upon Amasai, who was chief of the captains, and he said, “Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse: peace, peace be unto thee, and peace be to thine helpers; for thy God helpeth thee.” Then David received them, and made them captains of the band.
And there came of the children of Benjamin and Judah to the hold unto David. [16]

entries.section: 3. The children of Benjamin and Judah in the hold

paragraphs.text: For the second time some of the children of Benjamin appear, but not alone as the first time, but in the company of some of the children of Judah, to go to David in the hold, under the leadership of the Spirit of the Holy God [18].

entries.section: 3. The children of Benjamin and Judah in the hold

paragraphs.text: And David went out to meet them... and said unto them,
“If ye be come peaceably unto me to help me, mine heart shall be knit unto you.
But if ye be come to betray me to mine enemies, seeing there is no wrong in mine hands, the God of our fathers look thereon, and rebuke it.” [17]

David had many reasons to doubt their intention, for he doubted their intention lest they should have pretended friendship, so that he would trust them, and then they would deliver him up to Saul, but Amasai affirmed to him the sincerity of their intention.

By his saying “if ye be come peaceably” he reveals that some had gathered to him with an insincere intention, perhaps to learn his plan and inform Saul of it. Moreover there gathered to him all those who were in distress, and everyone that was in debt, and every one that was bitter of soul (1 Sam 22:2). David’s doubt did not come from nothing, because some of them had earlier betrayed him (1 Sam 21-22).
The Psalmist often suffered from the lying of men, so that he said: “I said in my bewilderment, Every man is a liar” (Ps 116:11).

St. Jerome sees that every man is a liar in the sense that, as he behaves as a man who lies, he is thus to be sanctified, and the saying applies to him: “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High” (Ps 82:6); he no longer remains a liar. [The man of holiness becomes a god, and since he is a god, he ceases to be a man, so he does not utter falsehood [7].]

entries.section: 3. The children of Benjamin and Judah in the hold

paragraphs.text: Then the spirit came upon Amasai, who was chief of the captains, and he said,
“Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse.
Peace, peace be unto thee, and peace be to thine helpers.
For thy God helpeth thee.”
Then David received them, and made them captains of the band. [18]

What Amasai uttered by the inspiration of the Spirit, “Peace, peace be unto thee, and peace be to thine helpers,” is considered the greatest gift given to David, for it surpasses the word peace in English, since Shalom in Hebrew does not mean the absence of war, but the fullness of happiness and abundance of good things [8]. David enjoys this because God is on his side.
Amasai: perhaps he is Amasa the son of Abigail, David’s sister (1 Chr 2:17). His words were eloquent in expression, presenting a prophecy.

The secret of strength is the coming down of the Spirit of the Lord upon those who work for the sake of the Kingdom of God. By the work of the Holy Spirit who came upon Amasai, the chief of the captains, they declared their love and admiration and his faithfulness to David. David received them and made them heads of the armies. The Scripture ascribes to the Spirit bodily strength, as happened with Jephthah (Judg 11:29) and Samson (Judg 14:19), and wisdom, as with Bezaleel (Ex 31:3), and eloquence, as with Amasai, and knowledge of divine matters, as with the prophets, and spiritual gifts.

The Spirit of the Lord gives special gifts to the people of God: He gave Bezaleel artistic skill (Ex 31:1-5), and Jephthah skill in war (Judg 11:29), and David the ability to rule (1 Sam 16:13), and Zechariah the son of Jehoiada a prophetic word (2 Chr 24:20).

v We read of the children of Israel that they went out to fight with a heart filled with peace; in the midst of the very swords and the shed blood and the slain bodies, because they were thinking of the victory of peace, not of their own victory [9].
St. Augustine

entries.section: 4. The children of Manasseh support David

paragraphs.text: 19 And there fell some of Manasseh to David, when he came with the Philistines against Saul to battle: but they helped them not: for the lords of the Philistines upon advisement sent him away, saying, “He will fall to his master Saul to the jeopardy of our heads.” 20 As he went to Ziklag, there fell to him of Manasseh, Adnah, and Jozabad, and Jediael, and Michael, and Jozabad, and Elihu, and Zilthai, captains of the thousands that were of Manasseh. 21 And they helped David against the band of the rovers: for they were all mighty men of valour, and were captains in the host. 22 For at that time day by day there came to David to help him, until it was a great host, like the host of God.
And there fell some of Manasseh to David, when he came with the Philistines against Saul to battle: but they helped them not: for the lords of the Philistines upon advisement sent him away, saying,
“He will fall to his master Saul to the jeopardy of our heads.” [19]
What is recorded here in verses [19-22] we find in (1 Sam 29-30). God had prevented David from fighting against Israel when he was with the Philistines.

The men of Manasseh did not show the faith of Benjamin, nor the strength of Gad, nor the strength of the Spirit as in Judah and Benjamin, but they declared their acknowledgment of him when the Philistines rejected him.
When the world rejects our Christ from reigning over their hearts, we declare our acknowledgment of Him that He may reign within us.

entries.section: 4. The children of Manasseh support David

paragraphs.text: As he went to Ziklag, there fell to him of Manasseh, Adnah, and Jozabad, and Jediael, and Michael, and Jozabad, and Elihu, and Zilthai, captains of the thousands that were of Manasseh. [20]

entries.section: 4. The children of Manasseh support David

paragraphs.text: And they helped David against the band of the rovers: for they were all mighty men of valour, and were captains in the host. [21]
The raiders were from the Amalekites. David and his men were defending Israel against the Amalekites, because Saul did not pay attention to them, either through his weakness or his negligence.

entries.section: 4. The children of Manasseh support David

paragraphs.text: For at that time day by day there came to David to help him, until it was a great host, like the host of God. [22]
What a wonderful picture of the making of David king, for he is the person who gathered Israel together with one heart.

entries.section: 5. Some wished to turn the kingdom to him

paragraphs.text: 23 And these are the numbers of the bands that were ready armed to the war, and came to David to Hebron, to turn the kingdom of Saul to him, according to the word of the LORD. 24 The children of Judah that bare shield and spear were six thousand and eight hundred, ready armed to the war.
And these are the numbers of the bands that were ready armed to the war, and came to David to Hebron, to turn the kingdom of Saul to him, according to the word of the LORD. [23]
The tribes streamed toward David, each tribe taking its place in supporting David, especially in the army.

This is a symbolic picture of the believers who work in the Church of Christ, His one body, but not all the members have one work. Each has his own gift, which he uses according to the manifold grace of God. “For as we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office: so we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another” (Rom 12:4-5).

Perhaps the splendid example here is the men of Benjamin; they left the honorary appearances, since they were keeping guard over the house of Saul, and reckoned that to be of no use, and devoted their energy to service and building up with David. The sons of Benjamin became a living example for the rest of the tribes. As the Apostle Paul says: “mark them which walk so as ye have us for an ensample” (Phil 3:17), as he also said: “whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7).
The total of all who came to Hebron was 339,000, besides Issachar and those who came with Zadok.

entries.section: 5. Some wished to turn the kingdom to him

paragraphs.text: It is to be noticed concerning those who gathered to him: 1. The large number of those coming from east of the Jordan, who reach 120,000, that is, more than a third. 2. Many came from the north (Zebulun, Asher and Naphtali). 3. Few came from Benjamin, because they were with the house of Saul [29]. 4. Few came from Judah and Simeon, because many of them had been with David from the beginning, and perhaps they are the brethren who prepared the food [39].

Perhaps one of the factors that drove the tribes to resort to David was the fall of Saul into David’s hands and David’s refusal to stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed, despite Saul’s many attempts to kill him.

The tribe of Judah had begun by making David king in Hebron, and he reigned seven years and six months, and there was continual war between the house of Saul and the house of David (2 Sam 2-4); this is not mentioned in the Books of Chronicles.

entries.section: 5. Some wished to turn the kingdom to him

paragraphs.text: The children of Judah that bare shield and spear were six thousand and eight hundred, ready armed to the war. [24]

Some may ask: why did the tribes near and neighboring to him present relatively small numbers, the tribe of Judah presenting 6,800 soldiers and Simeon 7,100 warriors, while Zebulun presented 50,000 warriors, and the tribes east of the Jordan 120,000 fighters?

This does not mean that the near and neighboring tribes were less zealous or faithful than the tribes that were far away in location; rather, it is because they felt that they were within David’s reach, that he could ask whatever he wished and find them in his hands supporting him. On the other hand, these tribes were bound to host those coming from distant places. And perhaps these tribes did not wish to be a burden upon David.

entries.section: 6. Mighty men of Simeon are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: Of the children of Simeon, mighty men of valour for the war, seven thousand and one hundred. [25]

entries.section: 7. Levites and priests are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: 26 Of the children of Levi four thousand and six hundred. 27 And Jehoiada was the leader of the Aaronites, and with him were three thousand and seven hundred; 28 And Zadok, a young man mighty of valour, and of his father’s house twenty and two captains.
Of the children of Levi four thousand and six hundred. [26]

The Levites were exempt from military service (Num 1:47-50), but here, along with offering prayers, they volunteered by choice for the general conscription in those critical circumstances, to help with all their hearts in entering the battles for the establishment of David as king.

entries.section: 7. Levites and priests are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: And Jehoiada was the leader of the Aaronites (the Aaronites), and with him were three thousand and seven hundred; [27]
The priests were called Aaronites because they were of the seed of Aaron.

entries.section: 7. Levites and priests are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: And Zadok, a young man mighty of valour, and of his father’s house twenty and two captains. [28]
Zadok: he was a faithful servant of David all his life, and he was the high priest at the beginning of Solomon’s reign.

entries.section: 8. Some of the guard of the house of Saul are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: And of the children of Benjamin, the kindred of Saul, three thousand (for hitherto the greatest part of them had kept the ward of the house of Saul). [29]
The number is smaller than the rest of the tribes, perhaps because some were afraid lest David should avenge himself because of Saul’s continual opposition to him and his attempt to kill him.

entries.section: 9. Mighty men of the children of Ephraim are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: And of the children of Ephraim twenty thousand and eight hundred, mighty men of valour, and famous in the houses of their fathers. [30]

These were marked by being mighty men of valor like many who came from the other tribes [25, 28, 30], but these were men of standing, so they did not attach themselves in greed to obtain positions in the state.

entries.section: 10. Some of the half tribe of Manasseh are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: And of the half tribe of Manasseh eighteen thousand, which were expressed by name, to come and make David king. [31]

[Which were expressed by name, to come and make David king]. How wonderful was what the tribe of Manasseh did: there was no quarrel or rivalry among those who go to make David king, but they were designated by name, since their gifts and works and zeal revealed their fitness for this mission.

entries.section: 11. The children of Issachar are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: And of the children of Issachar, which were men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do; the heads of them were two hundred; and all their brethren were at their commandment. [32]

This tribe presented the smallest number that any tribe presented, which is 200 leaders. But these leaders from the tribe of Issachar were marked as experienced in issuing wise decisions for the nation suited to that age, having understanding of the times [32]. For what suits one time may not suit another. This tribe specialized in managing the right time for uniting together and taking common action, especially the proclamation of making David king. Perhaps they were the thinking mind as to how to deal with Saul and his sons, and when to fulfil God’s true purposes concerning uniting together around David!

In the same spirit the Apostle Paul says: “And that, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed. The night is far spent, the day is at hand” (Rom 13:11-12).
They were known for prudence, counsel and wise discernment, so that the other tribes submitted to them, “and all their brethren were at their commandment” [32].
What a wonderful picture; we must submit in a spirit of love and humility to those to whom God has given this gift.

The work of God appears clearly in that Issachar’s taking this role did not cause the other tribes to be jealous of them; rather it was said next, and the men of Zebulun going out to war. And likewise the men of Asher bear the same spirit.

entries.section: 12. The children of Zebulun are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: Of Zebulun, such as went forth to battle, expert in war, with all instruments of war, fifty thousand, which could keep rank: they were not of double heart. [33]
The tribe of Zebulun was marked by readiness to go out to battle, supporting one another and keeping the order of their ranks; they did not know discord, but had one heart.
“Not of double heart”: the Hebrew expression means that they marched as one man, with one heart, and it is a military expression referring to military action organized in one spirit.

entries.section: 13. The children of Naphtali are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: And of Naphtali a thousand captains, and with them with shield and spear thirty and seven thousand. [34]
Naphtali closely resembles Judah, for they carry spears and shields, imitating the men who built the wall under the leadership of Nehemiah.

entries.section: 14. The Danites are drawn to him

paragraphs.text: And of the Danites expert in war twenty and eight thousand and six hundred. [35]
Both Dan and Zebulun are marked by standing ready for war. The men of Dan are drawn up in ranks as though awaiting the signal (2 Tim 1:7).
And of Asher, such as went forth to battle, expert in war, forty thousand. [36]

entries.section: 16. The east bank is drawn to him

paragraphs.text: And on the other side of Jordan, of the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and of the half tribe of Manasseh, with all manner of instruments of war for the battle, an hundred and twenty thousand. [37]

The tribes dwelling east of the Jordan came in great numbers; they crossed the river, and although they dwelt in a distant place, they passed over the river with the weapons of war. They came with one heart, for a spirit of brotherly love prevailed among all the tribes.

38 All these men of war, that could keep rank, came with a perfect heart to Hebron, to make David king over all Israel: and all the rest also of Israel were of one heart to make David king. 39 And there they were with David three days, eating and drinking: for their brethren had prepared for them. 40 Moreover they that were nigh them, even unto Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, brought bread on asses, and on camels, and on mules, and on oxen, and food of meal, cakes of figs, and bunches of raisins, and wine, and oil, and oxen, and sheep abundantly: for there was joy in Israel.
All these men of war, that could keep rank, came with a perfect heart to Hebron, to make David king over all Israel.
And all the rest also of Israel were of one heart to make David king. [38]

The number of these divisions reached more than three hundred thousand men, whose aim was to support David and establish him as king. Since David’s heart was upright, God gave him leaders possessing different gifts and experiences from all the tribes, working with one spirit, one aim, and one mind.

The tribe, the number presented and their gift: Judah, Simeon, Levi, Benjamin, Ephraim, half of Manasseh, Issachar, Zebulun, Naphtali, Dan, Asher, Reuben and Gad and half of Manasseh. 6,800 soldiers, bearers of shields and spears. 7,100 warriors, strong in war. 4,600 Levites. 3,000 of Saul’s kinsmen. 20,800 strong warriors. 18,000 for the enthronement of David as king. 200 of the chiefs, experienced and wise in managing the affairs of the state. 50,000 faithful warriors with every kind of weapon. 1,000 captains and 37,000 warriors with shields and spears. 28,600 fighters in the battles. 40,000 conscripted fighters in the battles. 120,000 fighters with every kind of weapon. [East of the Jordan].
Each tribe presented, according to its gifts and abilities, those who would help David in his establishment as king.

St. Jerome comments on the warriors with a perfect heart, or a heart filled with peace (a peaceful heart), in his exposition of Psalm 120: “Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps 120:2).

v “Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue,” not from the tongue of another person, but from my tongue. The tongue of another does not hurt me; my tongue is my enemy. Deliver me, save me from my tongue. My tongue is a sword that kills my soul. I think that I harm my enemy, and I do not realize that I am killing myself. My opponents may oppose me when I speak with them, but I will speak peace. Their spirit may be hostile to me, but let our spirit be for the peacemakers. It is written in Paralipomenon: “(The children of Israel) came with a perfect heart (filled with peace) to fight” (see 1 Chr 12:38) [10].

St. Jerome This celebration was an unusual one, “for there was joy in Israel.” The secret of their joy is that he represents the Messiah, the Savior of the world; they saw in him the shadow of salvation, and they enjoyed the spirit of praise, and realized that the word of God and the divine promises are the source of their surpassing joy.
And there they were with David three days, eating and drinking: for their brethren had prepared for them. [39]
Eating and drinking: meaning that the tribes, even in their eating and drinking, shared together as one family.

Moreover they that were nigh them, even unto Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, brought bread on asses, and on camels, and on mules, and on oxen, and food of meal, cakes of figs, and bunches of raisins, and wine, and oil, and oxen, and sheep abundantly: for there was joy in Israel. [40]

If all the tribes presented leaders in wars and in politics and in managing the affairs of the kingdom, the clans of the nearby tribes presented provisions in abundance, in the spirit of joy that pervaded Israel because of their leader, the man of God, David the prophet and king and sweet psalmist and judge.
The secret of their joy was not political capabilities and experience and material supplies, but the sense of the divine presence that gives joy.

“There was joy in Israel” (1 Chr 11:40). Some see that this expression is not the ordinary joy because of the enthronement of the king. It is the same joy that they enjoy in celebrating the Jewish New Year, in which Orthodox Jews still dance rejoicing in the Torah.

The secret of their joy is their gathering together in a spirit of harmony and unity without disputes or rivalry. This together with the sense that David was anointed by the Lord Himself to be king over all Israel.
The tribes had suffered grief for a time because of Saul’s rebellion against the Lord and his opposition to David, so they were broken before the Philistines and Saul and his sons died.
David rejoiced when he saw all the tribes united and in harmony, instead of divisions and civil wars.

Many of the tribes did not forget to bring food on asses and camels and mules, and with the food wine, which indicates a joyful atmosphere. For all carry the spirit of striving earnestly, and satisfaction and joy with brotherly love and unity, “for there was joy in Israel” [40].

The secret of strength in these tribes is the following: 1. The gathering of this great number for the sake of the glory of God. 2. Despite their large number and the large number of their varied divisions, they had one aim. 3. They presented abilities in abundance. 4. Joy had pervaded all the people! Now that Israel was united around the king whom the Lord Himself had appointed, they were in great joy. They gathered together around the good Shepherd.
v “Shout for joy in the LORD, O ye righteous: praise becometh the upright” (Ps 33:1).

We often hear of shouts of exultation in the Holy Bible, which express the state of the soul that is very happy and filled with joy. Not because everything is going well, and not for the sake of bodily health, nor because the fields have brought forth fruits of every kind, but because you have possessed the Lord. For He is beautiful and good and wise. Is not this joy with which He has filled you enough for you...

This text urges the righteous to realize the measure of their dignity, in that they have been counted worthy to be of the flock of this Teacher, and to feel pride as they serve Him. They have been filled with joy unspeakable, as they stand as though their hearts were rushing in the zeal of the beloved toward the loving God.

If you feel in your heart such a light as generates in you a comprehensive knowledge toward God, if God enlightens your heart that you may love Him, your concern for the world and its material things grows less. By this obscure brief sense you can perceive the full fullness of the righteous, who draw their happiness from God continually and without ceasing.

Rarely do you feel this sense, which is given to you by God’s dispensation. By this sense you return and remember what you lack. But the righteous man feels this continual divine happiness, because the Spirit dwells in him, and the first fruits of the Spirit are “love, joy, peace” (Gal 5:22).

“Shout for joy in the LORD, O ye righteous” (Ps 33:1). The God of the righteous dwells in the souls that are able to contain Him, and he in whom He dwells is marked by courage. And the righteous man rejoices and becomes a dwelling for the Lord when he receives Him in his heart. But he who sins leaves the place to the devil, and shuts his ear against hearing those words: “Neither give place to the devil” (Eph 4:27), nor those that came in the Book of Ecclesiastes: “If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee... leave not thy place” (Eccl 10:4). May we look, as far as we are able, to the Lord, and store up joy in our hearts, as we meditate on these words: “praise becometh the upright” (Ps 33:1) [11].
St. Basil the Great
Let the weak say, I am a hero!
v Because of Saul, David found no place for himself among his people.
He fled to the Philistines, and one of their kings gave him a city.
He hid in the city of Ziklag, but his movements were not completely secret.
In the midst of this distress, and with his flight, the fragrance of godliness arose from him, and reached all the tribes.
Even some of those who opposed him longed to attach themselves to him.
Many withdrew, even from the heroic brethren of Saul and his guard, and went to him.
Around him came to be heads of armies with wonderful abilities.
v But our Christ, the Son of David, came down by His own will and the will of His Father.
He came down to us not to seek a city to take refuge in, but seeking our hearts as a throne for Himself.
Men and women and children and young people gathered around Him.
He made them kings and mighty men of valor.
They continually chant the spiritual military hymn:
“Let the weak say, I am a hero” (Joel 3:10).
v The battlefield is our hearts, and its way is our Christ.
Our weapon is the cross of our Savior, and the secret of our victory is the abundance of His grace.
Our eyes look toward the heavens.
But our enemy the devil is under our feet, with no authority over us.
Our wounds in the battle give forth splendor and glory.
Our fortress is the Physician of souls and bodies, the Commander of the battle!
We do not fear death, because by His death He shattered the bars of Hades.
Nor do we fear the grave, because we meet the Giver of resurrection and immortality and incorruption.
v The army of salvation includes believers of the Old and New Testaments.
It includes warriors from all peoples and nations and tongues.
Its teaching is divine love and brotherly love.
Its victory is a crossing over to heaven!
v Our weapon is repentance in the spirit of hope, and humility in the spirit of certainty in God, and enjoyment of God’s grace without slackness and laziness on our part!
v In the midst of the battle our souls are filled with joy and exultation.
Those coming from unbelief to faith cling to us.
And the corrupt who put off the garment of corruption and put on the righteousness of Christ.
v Our battle knows no laxity or negligence.
In the midst of earnestness our Commander pours His sweetness into our hearts.
He opens our insight, so we enjoy the earnest of heaven.
Our battle with the devil will not cease as long as we are in the body.
Our battle with him stands between him and every believer!
But in truth we are not a party in it, for it is the battle of our Christ against the devil.
v Our Christ, the wonderful Commander, turned the battle of the cross into a wedding.
He offered His shed blood as a dowry for His Church.
He stretched out His hands to take His Bride into His embrace.
In the midst of our battle the divine Commander is revealed; we see Him as the Bridegroom of heaven, the gladdener of hearts, the Giver of immortality, who shines upon us with His splendor eternally!
v Some of the sons of Gad set out to David.
They crossed the valleys of the east and the west, and gathered with him in the hold on the mountain.
Grant me to pass over all the pleasures of the world and its afflictions.
And to set out to You, O Son of David, to meet You on the mountain.
On Mount Tabor You open my eyes, and I enjoy the mysteries of Your glory.
The lusts of the world do not draw me, nor am I troubled by its vexations.
You reflect Your splendor upon my depths, and establish Your Kingdom within me, so I comprehend the mysteries of Your divinity, and experience the earnest of Your heavens.
That I may meet You on the mountain, while You speak with the multitudes.
I hear Your sweet voice, and experience the power of Your word.
I hold fast to Your commandment, and so escape all the snares of the enemy.
I meet You on Mount Golgotha, the mountain of the wedding.
I cry out as with Dismas the thief:
Remember me, O Bridegroom of my soul, when You come in Your Kingdom!

entries.section: 1. A conversation with Nathan the prophet

paragraphs.text: 1 Now it came to pass, as David sat in his house, that David said to Nathan the prophet, “Lo, I dwell in an house of cedars, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD remaineth under curtains.” 2 Then Nathan said unto David, “Do all that is in thine heart; for God is with thee.” 3 And it came to pass the same night, that the word of God came to Nathan, saying,

entries.section: 1. A conversation with Nathan the prophet

paragraphs.text: The Lord affirms that the kingdom of David and the kingdom of Solomon are merely a share in the kingdom of God Himself, for the Lord says: “I will settle him in mine house and in my kingdom for ever” [14]. In (2 Chr 9:8) the true King of Israel is God Himself.
Our Lord directed Nathan to tell David that he was not the man chosen for this work.
Now it came to pass, as David sat in his house, that David said to Nathan the prophet,
“Lo, I dwell in an house of cedars, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD remaineth under curtains.” [1]

The book often repeats the prophecy of Nathan recorded in (2 Sam 7), and in its view it is of great importance. For it expresses the covenant made between God and David, and the continuity of his royal line, until the Son of David came, the eternal King.

David’s heart was aflame with love for God, so he could not bear to have a splendid palace while the ark of the covenant was placed in a tent. Therefore he wished to build a temple for the Lord. But everything has its own appointed time with the Lord. When David felt settled in the palace he had built, he wanted to build a house for the Lord in which the ark of the covenant would be placed. David’s mind was not at ease that he himself should dwell in a house of cedar while the ark was placed in a tent.

Look at David’s concern and his undertakings when his wealth increased and his power grew great. He did not think about what to do for his sons so as to share the wealth with them, or how to fill his treasuries and extend his authority, but rather he thought about what he might do to serve and glorify God.
Thus it is fitting for us to care for the service of the Kingdom of God in the world, and for His Church.

entries.section: 1. A conversation with Nathan the prophet

paragraphs.text: Then Nathan said unto David, “Do all that is in thine heart; for God is with thee.” [2]

As soon as Nathan the prophet learned of David’s desire, he said to him, “Do all that is in thine heart; for God is with thee,” because he had not the slightest doubt that God was with David. It is the duty of God’s servants to stir up, in themselves and in others, the movement of the grace and the gifts that are in them.

entries.section: 1. A conversation with Nathan the prophet

paragraphs.text: And it came to pass the same night, that the word of God came to Nathan, [3]

Some commentators (for example J. H. Blunt) see that Nathan the prophet’s advice was modified after the word of God came to him that night, since it is possible that the prophets were not always under divine inspiration, and could speak in some matters under the influence of their own human thought alone.

entries.section: 2. God accompanies His people wherever they are

paragraphs.text: 4 “Go and tell David my servant, Thus saith the LORD, Thou shalt not build me an house to dwell in: 5 For I have not dwelt in an house since the day that I brought up Israel unto this day; but have gone from tent to tent, and from one tabernacle to another. 6 Wheresoever I have walked with all Israel, spake I a word to any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to feed my people, saying, Why have ye not built me an house of cedars?
“Go and tell David my servant,
Thus saith the LORD, Thou shalt not build me an house to dwell in: [4]

God’s answer to David’s request came thus: David does not build this house; rather he prepares for it and does not build it, just as Moses brought the people of Israel near to Canaan, but left Joshua to bring them into it. It is the right of the Lord Christ alone to be the head of His work and the one who completes it.

entries.section: 2. God accompanies His people wherever they are

paragraphs.text: God condescends and accepts the good opinions of His people, even if He prevents them from carrying them out. He sent Nathan the prophet to comfort David’s heart and to say to him: 1. O David, your promotion to the high office was not in vain. I took you from the sheepfold, from following the sheep, not to build the temple, but to be ruler over my people Israel, and this is honor enough for you. Leave the building to another who will come after you [7]. Why should anyone think that he does everything and brings every good work to completion? Let him leave something for those who succeed him. For God gave David victories and made him a name [8], and above that He determined through him to appoint a place for His people Israel and to fortify it against its enemies; that must be his work as a man of war, and he must leave the building of churches to one who was never appointed to be a soldier. 2. O David, do not think that your good purpose has been in vain, or that you will lose its reward; for although I forbid you to carry it out, you will be rewarded as though you had done it, [for the Lord will build you an house, and will join the crown of Israel to it] [10]; for when there is a good will, it is not only accepted but also rewarded. 3. O David, do not think that I forbid you to do this great work so that it is never accomplished and that your thinking about it has been in vain; for I will raise up your seed, and he shall build me an house [11-12]. The temple of God will be built at the appointed time, even if we do not have the honor of helping to build it or the joy of seeing it completed. 4. O David, you must not confine your thoughts to the worldly prosperity of your family, but comfort yourself with the kingdom of the expected Messiah, for He is the one who comes from your loins and whose throne will be established for ever [14]. Solomon himself was not settled in the house of God as he ought to have been, and his family was not established in the kingdom: “But there shall come of your seed whom I will establish in my kingdom.” This means that he will be high priest over the house of God, and to him alone will belong authority over the works of the kingdom of God among men, and all power in heaven and on earth, in the house and in the kingdom, in the Church and in the world; so he will be a priest upon his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both, and he shall build the temple of the LORD (Zech 6:12-13).

entries.section: 3. God did not ask for a house for the ark, but a tent

paragraphs.text: For I have not dwelt in an house since the day that I brought up Israel unto this day; but have gone from tent to tent, and from one tabernacle to another. [5]
The time had not yet come to set the ark in a house of the Lord.

entries.section: 3. God did not ask for a house for the ark, but a tent

paragraphs.text: Wheresoever I have walked with all Israel, spake I a word to any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to feed my people, saying, Why have ye not built me an house of cedars? [6]

God does not want outward show, pomp and splendor in His service. His ark of the covenant was content with a tent, and He did not ask for a house to be built for Him, even after God had given His people rest in great and goodly cities which they built not (Deut 6:10). He commanded the judges to feed His people, but He never asked them to build Him a house [6]. May we sometimes be content with humble comforts, as the ark of God was.

entries.section: 3. God’s pleasure in raising up leaders

paragraphs.text: Now therefore thus shalt thou say unto my servant David,
Thus saith the LORD of hosts,
I took thee from the sheepcote, even from following the sheep, that thou shouldest be ruler over my people Israel: [7]

entries.section: 3. God’s pleasure in raising up leaders

paragraphs.text: And I have been with thee whithersoever thou hast walked, and have cut off all thine enemies from before thee, and have made thee a name like the name of the great men that are in the earth. [8]
This is God’s pleasure: to raise up every human being as a leader over his feelings, thoughts, words and conduct, so that he walks in a spirit of confidence and not of fear.

St. Cyril sees that those who do not fear God are not worthy that the psalmist should mention their names with his lips [4], but God mentions the name of the poor man with His tongue (Lk 16:19, 20) [1]. He is great in the eyes of God, and God makes him great before the heavenly beings and the sons of men.

entries.section: 4. His pleasure in the rest of His people

paragraphs.text: Also I will ordain a place for my people Israel, and will plant them, and they shall be moved no more; neither shall the children of wickedness waste them any more, as at the beginning, [9]

entries.section: 5. His pleasure in building a house for those He loves

paragraphs.text: 10 And since the time that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel. Moreover I will subdue all thine enemies. Furthermore I tell thee that the LORD will build thee an house. 11 And it shall come to pass, when thy days be expired that thou must go to be with thy fathers, that I will raise up thy seed after thee, which shall be of thy sons; and I will establish his kingdom. 12 He shall build me an house, and I will stablish his throne for ever.
And since the time that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel, I will subdue all thine enemies. Furthermore I tell thee that the LORD will build thee an house [10]

Scripture says of the two midwives who refused to kill the male children of the sons of Israel: “And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses” (Ex 1:21). Does God make houses?! Since the two midwives signify the Holy Bible, when it is studied with the fear of God and the believers live it as they ought, God establishes a place for the Scripture in many places; that is, the field of service opens and houses are raised up for God. Thus the world needs to see in us the word of God working in our heart with godly fear, so that the Gospel finds a place in every heart. Origen [2] sees in the two midwives “knowledge,” which supports the children of God in the birth of males as well as females, that is, in their having fruit in divine intellectual contemplation and in the sanctification of the emotions. For the males signify the intellect and the females the emotions. The two midwives also signify the Holy Bible with its two Testaments, Old and New, through which the children of God enjoy increasing fruit, intellectual and emotional, or spiritual and bodily.

entries.section: 5. His pleasure in building a house for those He loves

paragraphs.text: And it shall come to pass, when thy days be expired that thou must go to be with thy fathers, that I will raise up thy seed after thee, which shall be of thy sons; and I will establish his kingdom. [11]

entries.section: 5. His pleasure in building a house for those He loves

paragraphs.text: He shall build me an house, and I will stablish his throne for ever. [12]
Although David was obliged to enter into many battles for the stability and safety of the people, the Lord did not allow him to build the temple, because his hands had shed much blood.

entries.section: 5. His pleasure in building a house for those He loves

paragraphs.text: Who is this who builds a house for God and whose throne endures for ever, if not the Lord Christ, the Son of David, who built His Church upon the rock? Eusebius of Caesarea sees that [13] cannot apply to Solomon, but to Christ, the King of Peace.

v There is no doubt that Solomon was the son of David and his successor in the kingdom. And he was the first to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, and perhaps the Jews understand that he is the subject of the prophecy. But we rightly ask them whether the oracle applies to Solomon, which says: “I will stablish his throne for ever” [12]. And also, where did God swear with assurance by His holiness, as He foretells concerning his throne that it should be as the sun and the days of heaven?
